These birds are found in wetlands, salt ponds, and coastal areas where they can be seen gracefully stepping through the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their extraordinarily long legs are proportionally longer than almost any other bird group, and avocets have distinctive upward-curved bills while stilts have straight bills. Both have bold black and white plumage patterns that make them easily recognizable.
children.funFact: Black-necked Stilts have such long legs that they must bend them awkwardly or even kneel down to reach the ground when feeding on land.

children.name: Haematopodidae
Haematopus
children.description: Oystercatchers are large, stocky shorebirds known for their distinctive bright orange bills and bold black and white plumage. These specialized coastal birds are perfectly adapted for life along rocky shores and sandy beaches, where they use their powerful bills to pry open shellfish and probe for marine worms. They're often seen walking confidently along the water's edge, their sturdy legs carrying them over slippery rocks and through shallow surf.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Oystercatchers stand out from other shorebirds with their massive, chisel-like orange bills that are perfectly shaped for opening shellfish. Their large size, bold contrasting plumage, and loud, piping calls make them unmistakable among coastal birds.
children.funFact: Despite their name, oystercatchers rarely eat oysters - they prefer mussels, clams, and marine worms, and some individuals specialize in being either 'hammerers' who smash shells open or 'stabbers' who slip their bills between shell halves.

children.description: Oystercatchers are distinctive shorebirds known for their robust build and specialized feeding habits. These coastal birds have strong, chisel-like bills perfectly adapted for prying open shellfish and other marine creatures. They're typically found along rocky shores, beaches, and mudflats where they hunt for their favorite prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Oystercatchers stand out from other shorebirds with their thick, bright orange or red bills, stocky bodies, and bold black and white plumage patterns. Their bills are uniquely flattened and blunt-tipped, quite different from the thin, probe-like bills of most other coastal birds.
children.funFact: Despite their name, oystercatchers rarely eat oysters - they prefer mussels, clams, and other shellfish that are easier to open with their powerful bills.

children.description: Shorebirds and allies are a diverse group of water-associated birds that includes the familiar sandpipers, gulls, and terns you see along New England's coasts and wetlands. Most members of this group are excellent fliers with long, pointed wings and are closely tied to aquatic environments, whether ocean shores, mudflats, or inland waters. They typically have webbed or partially webbed feet and bills specially adapted for their feeding habits.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other water birds, most charadriforms have a unique jaw structure and tend to be more agile fliers with narrower wings. Many species in this group are also notable for their elaborate courtship displays and complex social behaviors during breeding season.
children.funFact: Arctic terns, members of this group, make the longest migration of any bird, traveling roughly 44,000 miles annually from Arctic to Antarctic and back!

children.name: Anseriformes
Anatidae
Aythya
children.description: Scaups, Pochards, and Allies are diving ducks that spend most of their time on open water, diving underwater to feed on aquatic plants, seeds, and small animals. These medium-sized ducks are excellent swimmers and divers, often gathering in large flocks on lakes, ponds, and coastal waters. They have compact, rounded bodies that are perfectly adapted for their aquatic lifestyle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike dabbling ducks that tip forward to feed at the surface, these ducks completely submerge themselves to forage underwater. They also have legs positioned further back on their bodies, making them powerful swimmers but somewhat awkward on land.
children.funFact: Canvasbacks are considered the fastest-flying ducks in North America, capable of reaching speeds up to 70 miles per hour during migration!

children.name: Anser
children.description: Grey Geese are medium to large waterfowl that make up the genus Anser, representing the 'true geese' of the Northern Hemisphere. These hardy birds are known for their strong flight abilities and impressive seasonal migrations, often traveling thousands of miles between their breeding and wintering grounds. They typically have sturdy bodies, webbed feet for swimming, and bills adapted for grazing on grasses and aquatic plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike swans, grey geese have shorter necks and more compact bodies, while they're generally larger and have different bill shapes compared to ducks. Most species in this group show various combinations of grey, white, and brown plumage, often with distinctive facial markings or bill coloration.
children.funFact: Snow Geese can live over 20 years and return to the exact same nesting areas where they were born, sometimes traveling in massive flocks of tens of thousands during migration.

children.name: Cygnus
children.description: True swans are the largest members of the waterfowl family, known for their elegant long necks, powerful wings, and graceful swimming abilities. These magnificent birds are found on lakes, ponds, and wetlands across the Northern Hemisphere and parts of the Southern Hemisphere. All true swans share similar body structures and behaviors, including their distinctive curved necks and strong pair bonds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: True swans are much larger than ducks and geese, with longer necks that allow them to reach underwater vegetation that other waterfowl cannot access. Unlike geese, swans have more streamlined bodies and tend to be less vocal during flight.
children.funFact: Despite their reputation for being silent, most swan species are actually quite vocal - the Trumpeter Swan gets its name from its loud, trumpet-like call that can be heard over a mile away!

children.name: Anas
children.description: The genus Anas includes some of our most familiar dabbling ducks - those ducks you see tipping forward to feed underwater with their tails sticking up. These medium-sized waterfowl are excellent swimmers and strong fliers, commonly found in ponds, marshes, and coastal waters throughout New England. They're known for their ability to take off directly from water without needing a running start.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike diving ducks, Anas ducks feed primarily at the surface by dabbling and upending rather than completely submerging. They also have a distinctive iridescent wing patch called a speculum that flashes bright colors during flight.
children.funFact: Male Anas ducks are famous for their elaborate courtship displays, including head-bobbing, tail-wagging, and showing off their colorful plumage - the mallard's iconic green head being perhaps the most recognizable example.

children.name: Branta
children.description: Black geese are a group of waterfowl known for their distinctive dark plumage, especially on their heads and necks. These medium to large-sized geese are highly migratory, traveling thousands of miles between their Arctic breeding grounds and temperate wintering areas. They're commonly seen in New England during migration and winter months, often forming large, noisy flocks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other geese, black geese have predominantly dark heads and necks with contrasting white markings, rather than the lighter, more uniformly colored plumage of other goose groups. Their bills are typically shorter and more compact than those of grey geese.
children.funFact: The Barnacle Goose got its name from a medieval myth that these birds hatched from barnacles on driftwood, since people couldn't figure out where they disappeared to during breeding season in the remote Arctic.

children.name: Bucephala
children.description: Goldeneyes and Bufflehead are compact diving ducks known for their distinctive head shapes and bright golden or yellow eyes. These small to medium-sized waterfowl are excellent divers that feed underwater on aquatic invertebrates, small fish, and crustaceans. They're commonly seen on lakes, ponds, and coastal waters throughout New England, especially during migration and winter months.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this group have rounded, puffy heads that appear large relative to their body size, giving them their characteristic 'big-headed' appearance. Their bright golden or yellow eyes are particularly striking and help distinguish them from other diving duck species.
children.funFact: Common Goldeneyes are sometimes called 'whistlers' because their wings make a distinctive whistling sound during flight that can be heard from quite a distance.

children.name: Melanitta
children.description: Scoters are large, stocky sea ducks that spend most of their time in coastal marine waters, diving underwater to feed on mollusks, crustaceans, and other bottom-dwelling creatures. These hardy ducks are built for life in rough ocean conditions, with powerful wings and bodies designed for diving deep beneath the waves. All three scoter species can be found along New England's coastline, especially during fall and winter migrations.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Scoters are distinguished from other sea ducks by their generally dark plumage and robust, heavy bills adapted for crushing shellfish. Males typically show distinctive white patches or colorful bill markings that help identify each species.
children.funFact: Scoters can dive to depths of over 40 feet and stay underwater for up to a minute while foraging, using their wings to 'fly' through the water as they search for food on the ocean floor.

children.name: Mareca
children.description: Wigeons and allies are medium-sized dabbling ducks that feed primarily at the water's surface by tipping forward or grazing on land. These ducks are known for their distinctive whistling calls and compact, rounded bodies that make them excellent both in water and on land. All members of this group have relatively short, broad bills perfect for their mixed diet of aquatic plants and grasses.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other dabbling ducks, wigeons have shorter necks and more rounded heads, giving them a distinctive compact appearance. Their bills are also notably shorter and broader than most other ducks in their family.
children.funFact: American Wigeons are sometimes called 'baldpates' because the white stripe on the male's head resembles a bald spot, and they're known as 'poachers' because they often steal food from diving ducks that bring vegetation up from deeper water.

children.name: Spatula
children.description: Shovelers and Allies are a group of dabbling ducks known for their specialized feeding behaviors and bill shapes. These ducks are found in shallow wetlands where they feed by filtering small organisms and seeds from the water. All members of this group are migratory waterfowl that breed in northern regions and winter in warmer climates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The Northern Shoveler has an unmistakable oversized, spoon-shaped bill for filter feeding, while the teals in this group have smaller, more typical duck bills but share similar feeding and habitat preferences. They are generally smaller and more agile than other dabbling ducks.
children.funFact: Northern Shovelers can pump water through their bills up to 60 times per minute, using comb-like structures along the edges to strain out tiny crustaceans, seeds, and other food particles.

children.name: Somateria
children.description: Typical eiders are large, sturdy sea ducks that spend most of their lives in cold marine waters along northern coastlines. These robust diving ducks are perfectly adapted for life in harsh oceanic environments, with dense feathering and powerful builds that help them thrive in frigid waters where other waterfowl cannot survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Eiders are distinguished from other sea ducks by their distinctive wedge-shaped heads, thick necks, and specialized bills designed for crushing mollusks and crustaceans on the ocean floor.
children.funFact: Female eiders line their nests with incredibly soft down feathers plucked from their own bodies - this 'eiderdown' is so insulating and lightweight that it has been prized by humans for centuries as the ultimate filling for luxury bedding and cold-weather gear.

children.name: Mergus
children.description: Typical mergansers are fish-eating ducks with long, thin bills lined with tooth-like serrations that help them grip slippery prey. These diving ducks are perfectly adapted for underwater hunting, with streamlined bodies and legs positioned far back for powerful swimming. Both New England species are large waterfowl that prefer clear lakes, rivers, and coastal waters where fish are abundant.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other ducks, mergansers have narrow, serrated bills designed specifically for catching fish rather than filtering food from water or mud. Their bills are also slightly hooked at the tip, giving them an even better grip on their slippery prey.
children.funFact: Mergansers are sometimes called 'sawbills' because their serrated bill edges look like the teeth of a saw, making them incredibly effective fish-catching machines.

children.name: Tadorna
children.description: Typical shelducks are large, colorful waterfowl that bridge the gap between ducks and geese in both size and behavior. These distinctive birds are known for their bold plumage patterns featuring combinations of white, black, rust, and chestnut colors. They prefer coastal areas, salt marshes, and alkaline lakes where they feed on small invertebrates and plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Shelducks are larger and more goose-like than typical ducks, with longer necks and legs, and they often graze on land like geese. Their bright, contrasting plumage patterns and upright posture make them easily recognizable among other waterfowl.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'ducks,' shelducks actually nest in burrows, tree holes, or other cavities rather than building traditional nests, and both parents take turns incubating the eggs.

children.name: Lophodytes
children.description: Lophodytes is a genus containing just one species - the distinctive Hooded Merganser. These are diving ducks that specialize in catching fish and aquatic invertebrates underwater, using their streamlined bodies and webbed feet to pursue prey beneath the surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mergansers, Hooded Mergansers have a dramatic fan-shaped crest that can be raised or lowered, and they're much smaller than their Common and Red-breasted Merganser cousins.
children.funFact: Male Hooded Mergansers can instantly transform their appearance by raising their spectacular black-and-white crests, making their heads appear twice as large during courtship displays.

children.name: Clangula
children.description: Clangula is a genus containing just one species - the Long-tailed Duck, a distinctive sea duck that spends most of its time in marine waters. These ducks are known for their remarkable diving abilities and their dramatic seasonal plumage changes, with males sporting exceptionally long tail feathers during breeding season.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Long-tailed Ducks are unique among sea ducks for their extremely long, pointed tail feathers (especially in males) and their complex molting pattern that gives them different appearances throughout the year.
children.funFact: Long-tailed Ducks are among the deepest diving ducks in the world, capable of diving down to 200 feet underwater to hunt for mollusks and crustaceans on the ocean floor.

children.name: Histrionicus
children.description: Harlequin Ducks are a unique genus of sea ducks known for their striking plumage patterns and preference for turbulent waters. These compact, hardy waterfowl are specially adapted for life in fast-flowing streams and rocky coastal waters. The genus contains only one living species, making it quite exclusive in the duck world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Harlequin Ducks are easily distinguished from other sea ducks by their bold white stripes and spots contrasting with slate-blue and chestnut coloring in males, and their preference for rough, churning waters rather than calm lakes or ponds.
children.funFact: Harlequin Ducks are exceptional swimmers that can dive and navigate through white-water rapids and crashing ocean surf that would be impossible for most other waterfowl to handle.

children.name: Oxyura
children.description: Stiff-tailed ducks are a unique group of diving ducks known for their distinctive tail feathers that stick up at an angle, giving them their name. These compact, chunky ducks are excellent divers that feed underwater on aquatic plants, insects, and small crustaceans. They have large feet positioned far back on their bodies, making them powerful swimmers but awkward walkers on land.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other ducks, stiff-tailed ducks hold their tails erect above the water and have oversized bills relative to their head size. Their legs are positioned so far back that they can barely walk on land, instead pushing themselves along on their bellies.
children.funFact: Male Ruddy Ducks perform an elaborate courtship display where they beat their bright blue bills against their chests while making bubbles in the water, creating a drumming sound that can be heard from quite a distance.

children.name: Cairina
children.description: Muscovy Ducks are large, distinctive waterfowl known for their unique appearance and behavior. They are the only ducks in this genus and are easily recognized by their prominent red facial caruncles (fleshy growths) and their ability to perch in trees, unlike most other duck species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other ducks, Muscovy Ducks have distinctive red, warty skin around their faces and bills, and males can be significantly larger than females. They are also unique among ducks for their tree-roosting behavior and relatively quiet nature.
children.funFact: Muscovy Ducks are one of the few duck species that can actually fly well enough to roost in trees, and they're surprisingly quiet - they hiss and wag their tails instead of quacking like most ducks.

children.name: Dendrocygna
children.description: Whistling-ducks are a unique group of waterfowl that get their name from their distinctive high-pitched whistling calls. Unlike typical ducks, they have longer legs and necks, and they often perch in trees rather than staying on the water. They are social birds that form strong pair bonds and both parents help care for their young.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Whistling-ducks can be easily identified by their upright posture, long legs that extend beyond their tail in flight, and their characteristic whistling vocalizations. They also have broader, more rounded wings than most other ducks.
children.funFact: Whistling-ducks are one of the few duck species where males and females look nearly identical, and they're unusual among waterfowl because they often nest in tree cavities up to 30 feet off the ground.

children.description: Ducks, geese, and swans are waterfowl with webbed feet, waterproof feathers, and bills specially adapted for their aquatic lifestyle. They're excellent swimmers and many are strong fliers, found in lakes, rivers, marshes, and coastal waters throughout New England. This diverse family includes everything from tiny buffleheads to majestic trumpeter swans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other water birds, all members of this family have lamellae - comb-like structures along their bill edges that help them filter food from water. They also have a special gland near their tail that produces oil for waterproofing their feathers.
children.funFact: Many ducks and geese can sleep while floating on water by tucking one leg up and resting their head on their back, while keeping one eye open to watch for predators - a behavior called unihemispheric slow-wave sleep.

children.description: Waterfowl are aquatic birds perfectly adapted for life on and around water. They have webbed feet for swimming, waterproof feathers, and bills designed for their specific feeding habits - from dabbling at the surface to diving deep underwater.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other water birds, waterfowl have a special gland that produces oil to waterproof their feathers, and their young are precocial, meaning they can swim and feed themselves shortly after hatching.
children.funFact: Many waterfowl can sleep while floating on water by tucking one leg up and resting their head on their back, while keeping one eye open to watch for predators.

children.name: Pelecaniformes
Ardeidae
Ardea
children.description: The genus Ardea includes the largest and most impressive herons and egrets you'll encounter in New England's wetlands. These tall, elegant wading birds share a distinctive S-shaped neck that allows them to strike at fish and frogs with lightning speed. All members of this group are patient hunters that stand motionless in shallow water before spearing their prey with dagger-like bills.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ardea species are notably larger than other herons and egrets, with longer necks and legs that make them excellent waders in deeper water. Their size and powerful bills allow them to tackle bigger prey than their smaller heron relatives.
children.funFact: Great Blue Herons can strike at prey in just 1/10th of a second, and their neck vertebrae work like a spring-loaded mechanism to deliver this lightning-fast attack.

children.name: Egretta
children.description: Small egrets and herons in the genus Egretta are medium-sized wading birds known for their elegant appearance and graceful hunting style. These birds share similar body shapes with long, slender necks, sharp pointed bills, and long legs perfectly adapted for wading through shallow waters while hunting fish, frogs, and other aquatic prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their larger heron cousins, Egretta species are more compact and agile, often seen actively stalking through shallow waters rather than standing motionless. They typically have more delicate features and tend to be more social during feeding and roosting compared to Great Blue Herons.
children.funFact: The Little Blue Heron is actually white as a juvenile and gradually molts into its distinctive blue-gray adult plumage, allowing young birds to feed alongside Snowy Egrets without competition since they look nearly identical!

children.name: Botaurus
children.description: Bitterns are secretive, marsh-dwelling herons known for their incredible camouflage abilities and solitary nature. These brown-streaked birds have evolved to blend perfectly with cattails and other wetland vegetation, making them some of the most elusive waterfowl in New England. They prefer dense freshwater marshes where they hunt fish, frogs, and other aquatic prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other herons, bitterns have heavily streaked brown plumage and shorter necks, and they point their bills upward when threatened to mimic marsh vegetation. They also lack the white or gray coloring typical of most heron species.
children.funFact: The American Bittern produces one of the most distinctive sounds in the marsh - a deep, resonant 'pump-er-lunk' call that can be heard up to half a mile away and sounds more like a old water pump than a bird.

children.name: Butorides
children.description: Green-backed herons are small, compact wading birds that belong to the heron family but are much smaller than their great blue and great egret cousins. They have stocky builds with relatively short legs and necks, making them well-suited for hunting in shallow water along pond edges, streams, and wetlands. These solitary birds are known for their patient hunting style and secretive nature.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike larger herons that hunt in open water, green-backed herons prefer dense cover and are much more compact and stocky. They have distinctive greenish backs and are significantly smaller than other New England herons, typically hunching their necks when at rest.
children.funFact: Green herons are one of the few bird species known to use tools, dropping insects, twigs, or feathers onto the water surface to attract fish within striking range.

children.name: Nycticorax
children.description: Typical Night Herons are stocky, medium-sized wading birds known for their nocturnal hunting habits. These herons have shorter necks and legs compared to other herons, giving them a more compact appearance. They are patient hunters that often remain motionless while waiting for fish, frogs, and other aquatic prey to come within striking distance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike the tall, elegant herons in other genera, typical night herons have a hunched posture with shorter, thicker necks and relatively short legs. Their eyes are positioned more forward on their heads, an adaptation that helps with their nighttime hunting.
children.funFact: Night herons have excellent night vision thanks to a high concentration of rod cells in their eyes, allowing them to hunt effectively in low-light conditions when many other herons are roosting.

children.name: Nyctanassa
children.description: The genus Nyctanassa contains stocky, medium-sized wading birds known as yellow-crowned and Bermuda night herons. These birds are specialized nocturnal hunters that prefer coastal marshes, mangrove swamps, and wetlands where they hunt for crustaceans, especially crabs, along with fish and amphibians.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their black-crowned cousins, yellow-crowned night herons have longer legs, a more upright posture, and distinctive yellow crown stripes on their heads. They also have a preference for hunting crabs rather than fish, with specially adapted bills for cracking shells.
children.funFact: Yellow-crowned night herons have been observed using tools, dropping shells and hard objects from heights to crack open tough prey like crabs and mollusks.

children.description: Herons, egrets, and bitterns are long-legged wading birds that make their living hunting fish, frogs, and other aquatic prey in shallow waters. These elegant birds are perfectly designed for wetland life, with their dagger-like bills, flexible necks that can strike like lightning, and long legs that let them wade through marshes and shorelines. You'll find them standing motionless at water's edge, waiting patiently for the perfect moment to spear their next meal.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other long-legged water birds, herons and their relatives fly with their necks folded back in an S-curve rather than extended forward. They also have specialized powder down feathers that help waterproof their plumage and keep them clean while hunting in muddy waters.
children.funFact: Great blue herons can strike at prey faster than the human eye can follow, extending their neck and spearing fish in just 1/10th of a second!

children.name: Threskiornithidae
Plegadis
children.description: Plegadis ibises are medium-sized wading birds with long, curved bills perfectly shaped for probing in shallow water and mud for food. These elegant birds have dark, iridescent plumage that shimmers with bronze, green, and purple tones in the sunlight. Both species in this genus are skilled foragers that feed on aquatic invertebrates, small fish, and amphibians in wetland habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other ibis species, Plegadis ibises have distinctively dark plumage with metallic sheens rather than white or bright colors. Their bills are more slender and finely curved compared to the heavier bills of other ibis genera.
children.funFact: The two Plegadis species are so similar that they were once considered the same species and can only be reliably distinguished during breeding season when the White-faced Ibis develops distinctive white facial markings.

children.name: Eudocimus
children.description: White and Scarlet Ibises are medium-sized wading birds with long, curved bills perfectly shaped for probing in shallow water and mud. These elegant birds are known for their distinctive appearance and social feeding behavior, often gathering in flocks to hunt for crabs, fish, and other aquatic prey in marshes and coastal areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other ibis species, members of Eudocimus have relatively smooth, uniformly colored plumage as adults - either pure white or brilliant scarlet red. Their bills are also more slender and evenly curved compared to the heavier, more angular bills of other ibis groups.
children.funFact: White Ibises and Scarlet Ibises are so closely related that they can interbreed where their ranges overlap, producing offspring with beautiful pink and salmon-colored plumage.

children.name: Platalea
children.description: Spoonbills are large wading birds instantly recognizable by their distinctive flat, spatula-shaped bills that widen at the tip like a spoon. These elegant birds feed by sweeping their specialized bills side to side through shallow water, filtering out small fish, crustaceans, and aquatic insects. They're closely related to ibises but have evolved this unique feeding adaptation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The spoon-shaped bill is the defining characteristic that sets spoonbills apart from all other wading birds, including their closest relatives, the ibises, which have long, curved bills.
children.funFact: Roseate Spoonbills get their beautiful pink coloration from the carotenoid pigments in the crustaceans and other small creatures they eat - the more they consume, the pinker they become!

children.description: Ibises and spoonbills are large wading birds with long, curved or flattened bills perfectly adapted for their feeding style. They probe and sweep through shallow water, mud, and soft sediments to find small fish, crustaceans, insects, and other aquatic prey. These social birds often feed and roost in flocks, and many species display beautiful plumage colors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their distinctive bill shapes set them apart from other wading birds - ibises have long, thin, curved bills like forceps, while spoonbills have flat, spatula-shaped bills. Unlike herons and egrets, they typically feed by touch rather than sight, using their sensitive bills to locate prey.
children.funFact: Spoonbills feed by sweeping their bills side-to-side through the water like a scythe, snapping shut instantly when they detect prey - a feeding technique called 'tactile feeding' that works even in murky water where they can't see their food.

children.name: Pelecanidae
Pelecanus
children.description: Pelicans are large waterbirds known for their massive bills equipped with expandable throat pouches used for catching fish. These impressive birds are among the largest flying birds in North America, with wingspans that can reach up to 9 feet. They're skilled fishers that either dive from the air or scoop fish while swimming on the water's surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pelicans are easily distinguished from other waterbirds by their enormous bills with stretchy throat pouches that can hold up to 3 gallons of water. Their large size, long necks, and distinctive fishing behavior make them unmistakable among New England's coastal birds.
children.funFact: A pelican's throat pouch can hold more than twice as much as its stomach - they use it like a fishing net to catch multiple fish at once, then drain the water before swallowing their catch!

children.description: Pelicans are large waterbirds famous for their enormous pouched bills, which they use like fishing nets to scoop up fish and other aquatic prey. These social birds are often seen flying in formation along coastlines or floating together in groups on the water. All pelican species are skilled fishers that feed primarily on fish, though their hunting techniques vary between species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pelicans are unmistakable due to their massive bills with expandable throat pouches, which are much larger and more prominent than those of any other waterbird family. Their combination of large size, long neck, and distinctive pouch makes them impossible to confuse with other birds.
children.funFact: A pelican's throat pouch can hold up to 3 gallons of water and fish - that's more than three times what their stomach can hold!

children.description: Pelicans, herons, and allies are large to medium-sized wading and diving birds that are closely tied to aquatic environments. Most members of this group have long legs for wading in shallow water, long necks for reaching prey, and specialized beaks adapted for catching fish, frogs, and other aquatic animals. These birds are commonly found around wetlands, marshes, rivers, and coastal areas throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other waterbirds, members of this order typically have bare skin around their faces and throats, and many species have specialized throat pouches or expandable neck sacs. Their feet are either fully webbed (like pelicans) or have long, separated toes ideal for walking on soft marsh surfaces.
children.funFact: Great Blue Herons can strike at fish with lightning speed - their neck muscles can extend their head forward in just 1/10th of a second, faster than the human eye can follow!

children.name: Accipitriformes
Accipitridae
Buteo
children.description: Buteos are a group of medium to large hawks known for their broad wings and relatively short tails, which make them excellent soaring birds. These raptors are commonly seen circling high overhead on thermals, scanning the ground below for small mammals, reptiles, and other prey. They're among the most familiar hawks in North America and are often what people picture when they think of a typical hawk.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike the smaller, more agile accipiters (like Cooper's Hawks), buteos have broader wings and shorter tails that are perfectly adapted for soaring rather than quick maneuvers through dense vegetation. They also differ from falcons by having broader wings and typically hunting from perches or while soaring, rather than diving at high speeds.
children.funFact: The iconic screaming call often used in movies for eagles actually comes from a Red-tailed Hawk - a buteo - because Bald Eagles have a much weaker, chirping call that Hollywood finds less impressive!

children.name: Haliaeetus
children.description: Northern Sea-Eagles and Fish-Eagles are large, powerful raptors that specialize in hunting fish and waterfowl near coastlines, rivers, and lakes. These magnificent birds are among the largest eagles in the world, with broad wings perfect for soaring over water while searching for prey. They're known for their impressive fishing abilities and their association with aquatic environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other eagles, sea-eagles and fish-eagles have unfeathered lower legs (tarsi) and specially adapted talons for grasping slippery fish. They also have longer, broader wings than forest-dwelling eagles, making them excellent at soaring over open water.
children.funFact: Steller's Sea-Eagle is one of the heaviest eagles in the world, with females weighing up to 20 pounds and having a wingspan that can reach nearly 8 feet!

children.name: Astur
children.description: True goshawks and allies are agile forest hawks known for their incredible hunting skills and ability to navigate through dense woodland. These medium to large raptors have relatively short, broad wings and long tails that help them maneuver quickly between trees while chasing prey. They are specialized bird hunters, though they also catch mammals and other small animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this group have distinctive flight patterns with several quick wingbeats followed by short glides, and their eyes typically change from yellow in juveniles to bright red or orange in adults. They're built more compactly than other hawks, with shorter wings and longer tails relative to their body size.
children.funFact: These hawks are so skilled at flying through forests that they can pursue prey at high speeds through dense trees, making sharp turns around branches that would seem impossible for such large birds.

children.name: Circus
children.description: Harriers are slender hawks that hunt by flying low over open grasslands, marshes, and wetlands with their wings held in a distinctive V-shape. They have excellent hearing and rely on both sight and sound to locate prey like small mammals, birds, and frogs hiding in tall grass. These graceful raptors are known for their effortless, buoyant flight style as they glide back and forth across their hunting grounds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other hawks, harriers have owl-like facial discs that help focus sound to their ears, and they hunt primarily by flying low and slow rather than perching or soaring high. Their long, narrow wings and white rump patch are also distinctive field marks.
children.funFact: Male harriers are notorious polygamists and may mate with up to five females in a single breeding season, performing spectacular aerial courtship displays where they loop and dive through the sky.

children.name: Accipiter
children.description: True accipiters are a group of woodland hawks known for their incredible agility and hunting prowess in dense forests. These birds have evolved specialized features that make them perfectly suited for chasing songbirds and small mammals through thick trees and undergrowth.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Accipiters have short, rounded wings and long tails that give them exceptional maneuverability in tight spaces, unlike the broad wings of soaring hawks like Red-tails.
children.funFact: Accipiters are so agile that they can fly at full speed through dense forest, using their long tails like a rudder to make split-second turns around branches while chasing prey.

children.name: Ictinia
children.description: The genus Ictinia contains two species of small, graceful raptors known as kites. These birds are characterized by their buoyant, almost effortless flight style and their preference for catching insects on the wing. They have sleek, falcon-like builds with pointed wings that make them incredibly agile aerial hunters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other North American raptors, Ictinia kites are primarily insectivorous and rarely hunt mammals or birds. They can be distinguished from other kites by their smaller size, more pointed wings, and distinctive habit of catching prey while flying rather than from perches.
children.funFact: Mississippi Kites are remarkable long-distance migrants that travel over 4,000 miles from their North American breeding grounds to their wintering areas in South America, crossing the Gulf of Mexico in a single non-stop flight.

children.name: Aquila
children.description: True eagles are large, powerful birds of prey in the genus Aquila, known for their impressive size, broad wings, and exceptional soaring abilities. These majestic raptors are built for hunting medium to large prey, with strong talons and keen eyesight that can spot potential meals from great distances. They typically inhabit open landscapes like mountains, grasslands, and tundra where they can use their superior flight skills to hunt effectively.
children.distinguishingFeatures: True eagles are distinguished from other raptors by their fully feathered legs down to their toes, massive size, and distinctive broad, finger-like wing tips during flight. Unlike many hawks and other eagles, Aquila species have a more robust build and longer, more rectangular wings adapted for soaring over vast territories.
children.funFact: Golden Eagles can dive at speeds exceeding 150 mph when hunting, making them one of the fastest birds in North America, and their incredible eyesight is estimated to be 4-8 times sharper than human vision.

children.name: Buteogallus
children.description: Black Hawks and Allies are large, powerful raptors known for their broad wings and robust build. These hawks are primarily found in tropical and subtropical regions of the Americas, where they hunt from perches near water and wetland areas. They are skilled hunters that feed on a diverse diet including fish, reptiles, amphibians, and small mammals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other hawks, members of this genus have exceptionally broad, paddle-like wings and shorter tails, giving them a distinctive silhouette in flight. Their legs are notably long and strong, adapted for wading and catching prey in shallow water.
children.funFact: The Great Black Hawk that appeared in Maine in 2018 was thousands of miles from its normal range in Central and South America, creating a birding sensation as it was only the second confirmed sighting of this species in the United States.

children.name: Elanoides
children.description: Swallow-tailed Kites are elegant raptors known for their distinctive deeply forked tails that resemble a swallow's. These graceful birds of prey are expert aerial hunters, spending most of their time soaring effortlessly through the sky while catching insects, small reptiles, and amphibians on the wing.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their dramatic scissor-like forked tail and contrasting black and white plumage make them unmistakable among North American raptors. Unlike other kites, they rarely flap their wings and instead rely on thermal currents for almost effortless flight.
children.funFact: Swallow-tailed Kites are so agile in flight that they can drink water by skimming the surface of ponds and even eat their prey while soaring, never needing to land to feed.

children.name: Elanus
children.description: Elanus kites are small to medium-sized raptors known for their distinctive hovering flight behavior and elegant appearance. These birds of prey are characterized by their pointed wings, graceful flight patterns, and ability to hover motionless in the air while hunting for small mammals in open grasslands and fields.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other kites, Elanus species are primarily white and gray with distinctive black shoulder patches and have the unique ability to hover like a kestrel while hunting.
children.funFact: White-tailed Kites can hover perfectly still in mid-air for extended periods, earning them the nickname 'Holy Ghost bird' due to their ghostly white appearance and ethereal hovering ability.

children.description: Hawks, eagles, and kites are powerful daytime hunters with sharp, hooked beaks and strong talons designed for catching prey. These raptors soar through New England skies hunting everything from small rodents and birds to fish and larger mammals. They're known for their keen eyesight, which can be several times sharper than human vision.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike owls, these raptors hunt primarily during the day and have forward-facing eyes that provide excellent depth perception. They differ from falcons by having broader wings built more for soaring than high-speed pursuit.
children.funFact: A red-tailed hawk can spot a mouse from over a mile away, and their grip strength can be up to 10 times stronger than a human handshake!

children.name: Pandionidae
Pandion
children.description: Ospreys are large, fish-eating birds of prey that are found on every continent except Antarctica. They are specialized hunters that dive feet-first into water to catch fish with their powerful talons. These impressive raptors are known for building massive stick nests on platforms, dead trees, or human-made structures near water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ospreys are unique among raptors for their reversible outer toe that helps them grip slippery fish, and their ability to close their nostrils when diving underwater. They have distinctive white heads with dark eye stripes and dark brown wings that show a characteristic crooked or 'M' shape when soaring.
children.funFact: Ospreys have specialized scales on their feet and backwards-facing barbs on their talons that act like velcro to prevent fish from slipping away once caught.

children.description: Ospreys are large fish-eating birds of prey that are found near water bodies around the world. They are specialized hunters with unique adaptations for catching fish, including reversible outer toes and closable nostrils for diving. These impressive raptors are known for their distinctive fishing technique of plunging feet-first into water to catch their prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other hawks and eagles, ospreys have specialized feet with spiky pads and reversible outer toes that help them grip slippery fish. They also have unique nostrils that can close when diving and longer, narrower wings adapted for soaring over water.
children.funFact: Ospreys build massive stick nests that can weigh over a ton and be used for decades, with some nests growing so large they've been known to cause power outages when built on electrical towers!

children.description: Hawks, eagles, kites, and their allies are powerful daytime hunters with incredibly sharp vision that can spot prey from great distances. These birds of prey have strong, hooked beaks perfect for tearing meat and powerful talons for catching and killing their prey. Most species soar high on thermal air currents, using their excellent eyesight to scan the landscape below for food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike owls which hunt at night, these raptors are active during the day and have forward-facing eyes that provide excellent depth perception. Their feet have sharp, curved talons that lock automatically when they grasp prey, making them incredibly effective hunters.
children.funFact: A hawk's vision is up to 8 times sharper than human vision - they can spot a mouse from over a mile away!

children.name: Galliformes
Phasianidae
Chrysolophus
children.description: Ruffed Pheasants are a small genus of spectacular game birds known for their incredibly ornate plumage and long, flowing tails. These medium-sized pheasants are native to the mountains and forests of central China and Tibet, where males display brilliant golden, red, and iridescent colors during breeding season.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other pheasants, ruffed pheasants have distinctive cape-like neck ruffs that can be fanned out during displays, and their tails are exceptionally long and elaborately patterned with intricate barring.
children.funFact: Male Golden Pheasants have tail feathers that can grow up to 3 feet long - nearly two-thirds of their total body length!

children.name: Meleagris
children.description: Turkeys are large, ground-dwelling birds known for their distinctive featherless heads and necks, which can change color based on their mood and health. These impressive birds are native to North America and are famous for their elaborate courtship displays, where males fan out their tail feathers and strut to attract mates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Turkeys are distinguished from other game birds by their much larger size, their ability to dramatically change the color of their bare head and neck skin, and the male's distinctive beard of specialized feathers hanging from the chest.
children.funFact: Wild turkeys can fly at speeds up to 55 mph and run up to 25 mph on the ground, despite weighing up to 25 pounds!

children.name: Bonasa
children.description: Bonasa is a genus of medium-sized forest grouse known for their distinctive courtship displays and woodland habitat preferences. These birds are characterized by their mottled brown and gray plumage that provides excellent camouflage among fallen leaves and forest undergrowth.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Bonasa are distinguished from other grouse by their prominent neck ruffs (collar of feathers) and their preference for deciduous and mixed forests rather than open areas or coniferous woods.
children.funFact: Male Ruffed Grouse create their famous drumming sound not by beating their wings together, but by rapidly beating them against the air to create compression waves that can be heard up to a quarter mile away.

children.name: Phasianus
children.description: Typical pheasants are large, ground-dwelling game birds originally from Asia that have been widely introduced around the world. They are characterized by their long, pointed tails, strong legs for running and scratching in dirt, and striking sexual dimorphism where males are much more colorful than females.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other game birds, typical pheasants have extremely long, graduated tail feathers that can make up half their total body length. Males display brilliant iridescent plumage with distinctive white neck rings and colorful body patterns.
children.funFact: Male pheasants can have tail feathers up to 20 inches long, and they use these dramatic plumes in courtship displays while making loud crowing calls that can be heard over a mile away.

children.name: Canachites
children.description: Canachites is a genus containing specialized grouse that have adapted to life in northern coniferous forests. These compact, chicken-like birds are perfectly suited for surviving harsh winters in spruce and fir forests, where they feed primarily on conifer needles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other grouse, Canachites species have specialized digestive systems that allow them to survive almost entirely on conifer needles during winter months. They also lack the dramatic courtship displays and sounds typical of most other grouse species.
children.funFact: Spruce Grouse are so well-camouflaged and trusting of humans that early settlers called them 'fool hens' because they would often sit motionless instead of flying away when approached.

children.name: Alectoris
children.description: Rock Partridges are medium-sized game birds in the genus Alectoris, known for their robust build and preference for rocky, mountainous terrain. These ground-dwelling birds are characterized by their distinctive plumage patterns and their ability to run swiftly across steep, rocky slopes rather than fly when threatened.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rock Partridges can be identified by their bold black and white striped flanks, reddish legs and bills, and distinctive facial patterns with white throat patches bordered by black lines.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'rock' partridges, Chukars were originally native to Asia and the Middle East but have become so well-established in rocky areas of western North America that they're now considered an iconic game bird of the American West.

children.name: Gallus
children.description: Junglefowl are the wild ancestors of domestic chickens, featuring colorful plumage and strong ground-foraging abilities. These medium-sized birds are known for their distinctive calls and social behaviors, living in small flocks in their native habitats. They are excellent scratchers and spend much of their time on the ground searching for seeds, insects, and other food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other game birds, junglefowl males have prominent curved tail feathers and bright, colorful neck hackles. They also have distinctive fleshy combs and wattles on their heads that are more pronounced than those found in related species.
children.funFact: The Red Junglefowl was first domesticated over 8,000 years ago and is the direct ancestor of all domestic chicken breeds worldwide, making it one of the most economically important bird species in human history.

children.name: Pavo
children.description: Peafowl are large, spectacular birds in the pheasant family known for their brilliant plumage and impressive courtship displays. The males, called peacocks, are famous for their enormous, colorful tail feathers that they fan out in elaborate shows to attract females (peahens).
children.distinguishingFeatures: Peafowl are distinguished from other pheasants by their extraordinary size and the male's distinctive eye-spotted tail feathers called a train, which can span up to 6 feet wide when displayed.
children.funFact: A peacock's brilliant tail isn't actually made of tail feathers, but rather extremely long covert feathers that grow from the bird's back and can contain over 200 iridescent eye-spots called ocelli.

children.name: Syrmaticus
children.description: Long-tailed Pheasants are a group of large, ground-dwelling birds native to Asia, known for their extraordinarily long, ornate tail feathers. These impressive gamebirds are closely related to other pheasants but stand out due to their spectacular plumage and striking size.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other pheasants, members of this genus have exceptionally long tails that can be several feet in length, often with intricate barring patterns and elegant curves.
children.funFact: Reeves's Pheasant males have tail feathers that can grow up to 8 feet long - longer than the bird's entire body!

children.name: Coturnix
children.description: Typical Old World Quails are small, ground-dwelling game birds in the genus Coturnix. These compact birds are known for their secretive nature, preferring to run and hide in dense vegetation rather than fly when threatened. They have rounded bodies, short tails, and mottled brown plumage that provides excellent camouflage in grasslands and agricultural areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike New World quails, Coturnix species lack the distinctive head plumes or crests found on many American quail species. They are also smaller and more migratory than most other quail groups, with some species making remarkable long-distance journeys.
children.funFact: Japanese Quail were among the first birds to be sent into space, with several quail eggs successfully hatching aboard the Soviet Mir space station in 1990 to study the effects of zero gravity on bird development.

children.name: Lophura
children.description: Gallopheasants are a group of large, ground-dwelling birds in the pheasant family known for their spectacular plumage and ornate tail feathers. These Asian natives are popular in aviculture and have established small populations in parts of North America through escapes or releases from captivity. They prefer forested habitats where they forage on the ground for seeds, fruits, and insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Gallopheasants are distinguished from other pheasants by their particularly elaborate tail feathers and distinctive crest or facial wattles. Males typically display dramatically different coloration from females, with striking black, white, or metallic plumage patterns.
children.funFact: Male Silver Pheasants perform elaborate courtship displays where they spread their magnificent tail feathers in a fan while strutting and calling to attract females, similar to peacocks.

children.name: Perdix
children.description: Perdix partridges are small, plump ground-dwelling birds known for their mottled brown and gray plumage that provides excellent camouflage in grasslands and agricultural areas. These stocky gamebirds have short, rounded wings and prefer to run rather than fly when threatened, taking to the air only when absolutely necessary with their characteristic whirring wingbeats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Perdix partridges are distinguished from other partridge groups by their distinctive horseshoe-shaped chestnut patch on the belly and their preference for open farmland and grassland habitats rather than dense forests.
children.funFact: Gray Partridges form some of the largest family groups among gamebirds, with coveys of 15-20 birds huddling together in tight circles during cold winter nights to share body heat.

children.name: Lagopus
children.description: Ptarmigans are hardy grouse that live in cold, mountainous, and arctic regions. They are famous for their seasonal color changes, growing white feathers in winter for camouflage in snow and brown or mottled feathers in summer to blend with rocks and vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other grouse, ptarmigans have feathered feet that act like natural snowshoes, helping them walk on snow and keep warm in freezing temperatures.
children.funFact: Ptarmigans are one of the few birds that completely change color twice a year, molting their entire plumage to match the seasons.

children.description: Pheasants, grouse, and allies are ground-dwelling birds with sturdy bodies built for life on the forest floor and in open fields. These birds are excellent scratchers and diggers, using their strong feet to search for seeds, insects, and plant matter in leaf litter and soil. Most species prefer to walk or run rather than fly, though they can burst into powerful, short flights when startled.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other bird families, members of Phasianidae have heavily feathered legs and feet adapted for scratching, plus relatively small heads compared to their robust bodies. Males are often much more colorful than females and may sport elaborate tail feathers, crests, or other ornamental plumage.
children.funFact: This family includes the wild ancestors of our domestic chickens (junglefowl) and turkeys, making them some of the most economically important birds in human history.

children.name: Odontophoridae
Colinus
children.description: Bobwhites are small, plump ground-dwelling birds known for their distinctive whistled call that sounds like "bob-WHITE!" They are compact quail with short, rounded wings and prefer to run rather than fly when escaping danger. These social birds often gather in groups called coveys, especially during winter months.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bobwhites can be identified by their chunky, chicken-like build and their characteristic white throat patches contrasted with dark head markings. Unlike other quail species, they have a clear, musical whistle rather than harsh calls.
children.funFact: When threatened, a covey of bobwhites will explode outward in all directions in a startling burst called a "covey rise," with each bird flying off at a different angle to confuse predators before regrouping later by calling to each other.

children.name: Callipepla
children.description: Crested Quails are small, ground-dwelling game birds known for their distinctive forward-curving head plumes that look like little teardrop-shaped feathers. These chunky, short-tailed birds are excellent runners who prefer to scurry away from danger rather than fly, and they're often seen moving in small family groups called coveys.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other quail groups, Crested Quails have that signature forward-curving head crest that bobs as they walk. They also tend to be more colorful and patterned than many of their quail relatives, with intricate scaling and bold markings on their plumage.
children.funFact: California Quail perform adorable 'dust baths' where they wiggle and roll in dry dirt to clean their feathers and get rid of parasites - it looks like they're having a spa day!

children.description: New World Quails are small, ground-dwelling game birds found throughout the Americas. They are chunky, compact birds with short wings and legs, perfectly adapted for running through dense underbrush and scratching for seeds, insects, and other food on the forest floor. These social birds often travel in small flocks called coveys and are known for their distinctive calls.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their Old World relatives, New World Quails have serrated bills with tiny tooth-like projections along the edges, which is where their scientific family name Odontophoridae (meaning 'tooth-bearer') comes from. They also lack the leg spurs that many Old World quails possess.
children.funFact: When threatened, New World Quails perform a dramatic 'explosion' behavior where the entire covey suddenly bursts into flight in different directions, creating chaos that confuses predators and gives individual birds a better chance to escape.

children.name: Numididae
Numida
children.description: Numida is a genus of large, ground-dwelling birds known as helmeted guineafowl. These distinctive birds are characterized by their rounded bodies, bare heads and necks, and unique bony casques (helmet-like projections) on top of their heads.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other guineafowl, members of Numida have prominent bony helmets on their heads and distinctive wattled facial skin that can be brightly colored red, blue, or white.
children.funFact: Helmeted guineafowl are excellent natural pest controllers, consuming up to 2,000 ticks per bird each day along with other insects and small reptiles.

children.description: Guineafowl are distinctive ground-dwelling birds native to Africa, characterized by their rounded bodies, bare heads and necks, and spotted or striped plumage. These social birds are known for their loud, chattering calls and tendency to move in flocks while foraging for insects, seeds, and small animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other game birds, guineafowl have helmet-like casques or bony crests on their heads and colorful, unfeathered facial skin that can change color based on their mood or excitement level.
children.funFact: Guineafowl are excellent natural pest controllers and are sometimes kept on farms specifically to eat ticks, snakes, and other unwanted creatures.

children.description: Landfowl are ground-dwelling birds that prefer to walk and run rather than fly, though they can burst into short, powerful flights when threatened. These chunky, heavy-bodied birds spend most of their time foraging on the ground for seeds, berries, insects, and other small foods. They include familiar game birds like wild turkeys, ruffed grouse, and bobwhite quail.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other bird orders, landfowl have strong, scratching feet perfectly adapted for digging and foraging in soil and leaf litter. Their wings are short and rounded, built for quick escape flights rather than long-distance travel.
children.funFact: Many landfowl species perform elaborate courtship displays, like the male ruffed grouse's famous "drumming" where it beats its wings so rapidly it creates a thunderous sound that can be heard up to a quarter mile away.

children.name: Gruiformes
Rallidae
Rallus
children.description: Typical Rails are secretive, chicken-like marsh birds with laterally compressed bodies that help them slip through dense cattails and reeds. These long-billed waders are perfectly adapted for life in wetlands, using their slender bills to probe for small fish, crabs, and aquatic invertebrates. All three New England species are known for their elusive nature and distinctive calls that often betray their presence in seemingly empty marshes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other rail species, typical rails have long, slightly curved bills and are closely tied to saltwater or brackish marshes (except the King Rail which prefers freshwater). They're larger and more robust than most other rails, with stronger legs for wading through deeper water.
children.funFact: Rails have a saying among birders: 'thin as a rail' - their bodies are so laterally compressed they can actually squeeze through gaps narrower than you'd think possible, allowing them to navigate through the densest marsh vegetation.

children.name: Fulica
children.description: Coots are chunky, dark waterbirds that belong to the rail family but behave more like ducks. They have distinctive lobed toes instead of webbed feet, which help them swim and walk on floating vegetation. These birds are excellent divers and spend most of their time in marshes, ponds, and lakes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike ducks, coots have bright white bills and unusual lobed toes rather than webbed feet. They also bob their heads while swimming and must run across the water's surface to take flight, unlike most waterfowl.
children.funFact: American Coots are sometimes called 'mud hens' and are known for their aggressive territorial behavior - they'll chase away other waterfowl and even attack their own chicks if food is scarce!

children.name: Gallinula
children.description: Typical moorhens are medium-sized waterbirds that belong to the rail family, known for their dark plumage and distinctive white undertail coverts that flash when they walk or swim. They have strong legs with long, unwebbed toes that help them walk on floating vegetation and swim in marshes, ponds, and other wetlands. These birds are excellent at both swimming and walking, making them well-adapted to life in shallow water habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Moorhens can be distinguished from other rails by their bright red bills with yellow tips, red eyes, and prominent white patches under their tails that are visible when they flick their tails up while walking or swimming.
children.funFact: Despite not having webbed feet like ducks, moorhens are excellent swimmers and can even dive underwater to escape predators, using their wings to 'fly' beneath the surface.

children.name: Porzana
children.description: Spotted Crakes and their allies are small, secretive water birds that live in marshes, wetlands, and shallow water areas. They have compact bodies, long toes for walking on soft mud and floating vegetation, and short, rounded wings. These birds are masters of staying hidden among dense marsh grasses and reeds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are typically smaller and more slender than other rails, with shorter bills and more compressed bodies that help them slip through thick vegetation. They often have distinctive spotted or barred plumage patterns that provide excellent camouflage.
children.funFact: Despite being poor fliers with their short wings, these birds are capable of remarkable long-distance migrations, with some species traveling thousands of miles between breeding and wintering grounds.

children.name: Porphyrio
children.description: Swamphens and blue gallinules are large, colorful water birds in the rail family known for their vibrant blue and purple plumage and oversized feet. These marsh-dwelling birds are excellent swimmers and climbers, using their long toes to walk across floating vegetation in wetlands. They're omnivorous birds that feed on both plant matter and small animals in their aquatic habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other rails, members of Porphyrio are notably larger and more brightly colored, with striking blue, purple, or green iridescent feathers. They also have proportionally larger, more robust bills and feet compared to their more secretive rail relatives.
children.funFact: Purple Gallinules can use their incredibly long toes to walk across lily pads and other floating vegetation so skillfully that they appear to be walking on water.

children.name: Laterallus
children.description: Laterallus crakes are tiny, secretive rail birds that live in dense marsh vegetation and wet meadows. They are among the smallest members of the rail family, with mouse-like proportions and incredibly elusive behavior that makes them extremely difficult to spot in the wild.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These crakes are distinguished from other rails by their exceptionally small size, short tails, and tendency to run rather than fly when threatened. They have laterally compressed bodies that help them slip through dense vegetation like living shadows.
children.funFact: Black Rails are so secretive that they're sometimes called 'ghost birds' - they're more often heard than seen, and some birdwatchers go decades without ever glimpsing one despite hearing their distinctive 'ki-ki-kerr' call in the marshes.

children.name: Coturnicops
children.description: Coturnicops rails are small, secretive marsh birds that are among the most elusive members of the rail family. These compact birds have short bills and prefer to stay hidden in dense wetland vegetation, making them incredibly difficult to spot even when they're present.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Coturnicops rails are distinguished from other rails by their smaller size, shorter bills, and more quail-like proportions. They have a distinctive mouse-like behavior, scurrying through grass rather than walking openly like larger rails.
children.funFact: Yellow Rails are so secretive that they're sometimes called 'feathered mice' because they prefer to run through marsh grass rather than fly, and their calls sound like tapping two small stones together.

children.description: Rails, gallinules, and coots are secretive wetland birds that spend most of their time wading through marsh vegetation or swimming in shallow water. They have laterally compressed bodies (flattened from side to side) that help them slip through dense reeds and cattails, and long toes that distribute their weight when walking on floating vegetation. Most species are somewhat chicken-like in appearance with short, rounded wings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike ducks and other waterfowl, rails have lobed rather than webbed toes, and their bodies are compressed sideways rather than flattened top-to-bottom. They're also much more secretive than most water birds, preferring to skulk through dense vegetation rather than swim in open water.
children.funFact: The phrase "thin as a rail" comes from these birds' incredibly narrow body shape, which allows them to squeeze through marsh grass that looks too dense for any bird to navigate.

children.name: Gruidae
Antigone
children.description: Antigone cranes are large, elegant wading birds known for their impressive height, long necks, and distinctive dancing displays. These cranes are among the most widespread crane species in the world, found across North America and parts of Asia. They're highly social birds that gather in large flocks, especially during migration and winter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Antigone cranes are distinguished from other crane genera by their red crowns (bare red skin on top of their heads) and their generally gray plumage with rusty-colored patches. They also tend to be more adaptable to human-modified landscapes compared to other crane species.
children.funFact: Sandhill Cranes can live over 20 years and are known to mate for life, performing elaborate courtship dances that include leaping, bowing, and calling in unison with their partners.

children.name: Grus
children.description: Grus cranes are large, elegant wading birds known for their impressive size, long legs, and distinctive calls. These majestic birds are famous for their elaborate dancing displays during courtship and their ability to migrate thousands of miles between breeding and wintering grounds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Grus cranes are distinguished from other crane genera by their unfeathered red crown patches and their particularly loud, trumpeting calls that can be heard from miles away.
children.funFact: Grus cranes have been revered in many cultures for thousands of years and are considered symbols of longevity and good fortune, with some species known to live over 60 years in captivity.

children.description: Cranes are large, elegant wading birds known for their impressive height, long necks, and distinctive dancing displays. These majestic birds are found in wetlands, grasslands, and agricultural areas where they feed on a varied diet of plants, insects, small fish, and amphibians. They are highly social birds that often gather in large flocks during migration and are famous for their loud, trumpeting calls that can be heard from miles away.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cranes can be distinguished from similar birds like herons by their straight necks that remain extended during flight, rather than folded back. They also have longer legs relative to their body size and distinctive bare patches of red skin on their heads.
children.funFact: Cranes are among the oldest living bird families on Earth, with fossil evidence showing they have existed for over 60 million years, and many species mate for life and can live for several decades in the wild.

children.name: Aramidae
Aramus
children.description: Limpkins are large, long-legged wading birds that specialize in hunting apple snails in freshwater wetlands. They have distinctive brown plumage with white streaks and spots, and long, slightly curved bills perfectly adapted for extracting snails from their shells. These birds are most active during dawn and dusk when they wade through shallow waters searching for their preferred prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Limpkins are unique among wading birds for their specialized diet of apple snails and their haunting, wailing calls that echo through wetlands at night. Unlike herons or ibises, they have a distinctive jerky, limping walk that gives them their name.
children.funFact: The Limpkin is so specialized for eating apple snails that the tip of its bill is perfectly shaped to extract the soft snail body from its shell without breaking it.

children.description: Limpkins are unique wading birds that specialize in hunting apple snails in freshwater wetlands. They have long, slightly curved bills perfectly adapted for extracting snails from their shells, and their diet is so specialized that they depend almost entirely on these mollusks for survival.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other wading birds, limpkins have bills with a slight gap near the tip that allows them to cut the muscle holding a snail in its shell. Their streaked brown plumage and haunting, wailing calls also set them apart from herons and other wetland birds.
children.funFact: Limpkins are sometimes called 'crying birds' because their loud, mournful wails can be heard over a mile away, especially at night when they're most active.

children.description: Cranes, Rails, and Allies are a diverse group of wading and marsh birds that are perfectly adapted for life in wetlands. These birds share long toes that help them walk on soft mud and floating vegetation, plus strong legs for wading through shallow water. While they vary greatly in size from tiny rails to towering cranes, they all have a special fondness for wetland habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike herons and other wading birds, these species have more compressed bodies that help them slip through dense marsh vegetation. They also tend to be more secretive and skulking in their behavior, often heard but not seen.
children.funFact: Rails are famous for being able to 'run on water' - their long toes distribute their weight so well that they can literally sprint across lily pads and floating vegetation without sinking!

children.name: Strigiformes
Strigidae
Strix
children.description: Wood owls and allies in the genus Strix are medium to large owls that prefer forested habitats and hunt primarily at night. These owls are known for their distinctive facial discs, which help funnel sound to their ears for precise hunting, and their haunting hoots that echo through the woods. They typically nest in tree cavities and are skilled at catching small mammals, amphibians, and other prey in dense woodland environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other owl groups, Strix owls lack ear tufts and have particularly well-developed facial discs that give them a very round-headed appearance. They also tend to be more vocal than other owl genera, with complex hooting patterns that are often used for territory establishment and communication.
children.funFact: Barred Owls have been expanding their range westward and now compete with the closely related but larger Spotted Owls, sometimes even hybridizing with them to create 'Sparred Owls.'

children.name: Bubo
children.description: The genus Bubo includes the largest and most powerful owls in the world, characterized by their impressive size, prominent ear tufts, and fierce hunting abilities. These are the apex predators of the owl world, capable of taking prey much larger than other owl species. In New England, this group is represented by two magnificent species that showcase the diversity within this genus.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bubo owls are distinguished from other owls by their exceptional size, prominent feathered 'horns' or ear tufts, and incredibly powerful talons that can exert crushing force. Their deep, resonant hoots are among the most recognizable owl calls in nature.
children.funFact: Great Horned Owls have a grip strength of about 300 pounds per square inch in their talons - that's stronger than a large dog's bite and powerful enough to crush the bones of their prey!

children.name: Aegolius
children.description: Saw-whet owls and their allies are small, compact owls known for their distinctive calls and secretive nature. These woodland hunters have large heads relative to their body size and are perfectly adapted for nocturnal life in dense forests. Both New England species are skilled at catching small mammals and have excellent hearing to locate prey in complete darkness.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other small owls by their lack of ear tufts, their relatively short tails, and their distinctive facial disc patterns. They also have asymmetrically placed ear openings that give them exceptional directional hearing abilities.
children.funFact: The Northern Saw-whet Owl gets its name from its call, which early settlers thought sounded like a saw being sharpened on a whetstone.

children.name: Asio
children.description: The genus Asio includes medium-sized owls known for their prominent ear tufts and distinctive facial discs that help them pinpoint sounds in the dark. These owls are skilled hunters that primarily feed on small mammals like mice and voles, using their exceptional hearing and silent flight to catch prey. Both species in New England are somewhat nomadic, moving to areas where rodent populations are abundant.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other owl genera, Asio species have conspicuous ear tufts (though the Short-eared Owl's are very small) and relatively long wings adapted for sustained flight over open areas. Their facial discs are particularly well-developed compared to other owl groups, giving them an especially keen sense of hearing.
children.funFact: Long-eared Owls can make themselves look incredibly thin by stretching upward and compressing their feathers when trying to hide, transforming from a round, fluffy owl into what looks like a broken tree branch!

children.name: Megascops
children.description: Screech-owls are small to medium-sized owls known for their distinctive ear tufts and compact bodies. They are primarily nocturnal hunters that feed on small mammals, birds, and insects, and are well-adapted to both woodland and suburban environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike larger owl species, screech-owls have prominent ear tufts and are much smaller in size, typically 6-10 inches tall. They also have a distinctive trilling or whinnying call rather than the classic 'hoot' of larger owls.
