children.funFact: Despite their name, screech-owls don't actually screech - they produce soft trills, whinnies, and whistles that sound more musical than harsh.

children.name: Surnia
children.description: Surnia is a genus containing just one species - the Northern Hawk Owl. These medium-sized owls are unique among owls for their hawk-like appearance and daytime hunting behavior, making them quite different from most of their nocturnal relatives.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical owls, Northern Hawk Owls have a relatively small facial disc, a long tail, and pointed wings that give them a falcon-like silhouette in flight. They are also primarily diurnal (active during the day) rather than nocturnal.
children.funFact: Northern Hawk Owls can detect prey moving beneath snow from over half a mile away, and they often perch conspicuously on treetops like hawks rather than hiding like most owls.

children.description: Typical owls are the largest family of owls, including most of the species we're familiar with like great horned owls, screech owls, and saw-whet owls. These nocturnal hunters share specialized features like asymmetrical ear openings that help them pinpoint prey in complete darkness, and soft flight feathers that allow them to fly silently through the forest.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike barn owls, typical owls have round facial discs rather than heart-shaped ones, and their eyes are positioned more to the front of their heads. They also lack the comb-like serrations on their middle toe that barn owls use for grooming.
children.funFact: Many typical owls can rotate their heads up to 270 degrees because they have twice as many neck vertebrae as humans - 14 compared to our 7!

children.name: Tytonidae
Tyto
children.commonName: Barn, Masked, Grass, and Sooty Owls
children.description: The genus Tyto includes the barn owls and their close relatives, characterized by their distinctive heart-shaped facial discs and relatively long legs. These owls are found worldwide and are known for their exceptional hunting abilities, particularly their incredibly sensitive hearing that allows them to locate prey in complete darkness.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tyto owls can be distinguished from other owl groups by their prominent heart-shaped or monkey-like facial discs, which are more pronounced than in most other owl species. They also tend to have longer, more slender legs compared to typical owls.
children.funFact: Barn owls have asymmetrically placed ears - one higher than the other - which creates a slight time delay in sound reception that helps them pinpoint the exact location of prey with remarkable precision, even in total darkness.

children.description: Barn owls are a distinctive family of owls known for their heart-shaped facial discs and silent flight. These nocturnal hunters have excellent hearing and vision that helps them catch small mammals like mice and voles in complete darkness. They're found on every continent except Antarctica, making them one of the most widespread bird families in the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical owls, barn owls have heart-shaped rather than round facial discs, and their calls are more like screeches and hisses than hoots. They also have longer legs and a more upright posture compared to their round-faced owl relatives.
children.funFact: A barn owl can catch prey in total darkness using only its hearing - their asymmetrically placed ears create a 3D sound map that's so precise they can snatch a mouse without ever seeing it!

children.description: Owls are nocturnal birds of prey with specialized adaptations for hunting in darkness. They have large, forward-facing eyes for excellent night vision, asymmetrically placed ears for pinpoint hearing, and soft feathers that allow for silent flight. These skilled predators hunt small mammals, birds, and other creatures using their sharp talons and hooked beaks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other raptors, owls have large, round facial discs that help funnel sound to their ears, and their eyes are fixed in their sockets, requiring them to turn their entire head to look around. Their flight feathers have special fringed edges that eliminate the sound of air passing over their wings.
children.funFact: Owls can rotate their heads up to 270 degrees in either direction because they have 14 neck vertebrae compared to just 7 in humans!

children.name: Procellariiformes
Procellariidae
Ardenna
children.description: Southern Shearwaters are large, powerful seabirds that spend most of their lives gliding over the open ocean. These accomplished travelers breed in the Southern Hemisphere but migrate thousands of miles north to feed in New England's nutrient-rich waters during our summer months.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other shearwater groups, Southern Shearwaters are notably larger and darker overall, with long, narrow wings perfectly adapted for effortless gliding over ocean swells.
children.funFact: Great Shearwaters nest only on a few remote islands in the South Atlantic, yet they can be spotted off New England coasts just months later after completing one of the longest migrations in the bird world.

children.name: Calonectris
children.description: Large Shearwaters are impressive seabirds that spend most of their lives gliding over ocean waters with their long, narrow wings. These powerful fliers are built for life at sea, with streamlined bodies and tube-shaped nostrils that help them process salt water. They nest in colonies on islands and feed by skimming the surface or making shallow dives to catch fish and squid.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Large Shearwaters are notably bigger and bulkier than other shearwater species, with broader wings and more powerful flight. They have distinctively large, thick bills compared to their smaller relatives.
children.funFact: These marathon migrants can travel thousands of miles across entire ocean basins, with some individuals crossing from Europe to North America and back again each year.

children.name: Puffinus
children.description: Small Shearwaters are streamlined seabirds in the genus Puffinus that spend most of their lives gliding over ocean waters. These medium-sized birds have long, narrow wings that allow them to 'shear' close to the water's surface with minimal effort, rarely flapping as they search for fish and squid. They come to land only during breeding season, nesting in burrows on remote islands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Small Shearwaters are smaller and more compact than their larger relatives like the Great Shearwater, with distinctive black-and-white plumage patterns. They have a characteristic stiff-winged flight style, gliding in long arcs just above the waves.
children.funFact: Manx Shearwaters can live over 50 years and return to the exact same burrow site each breeding season, sometimes traveling thousands of miles from their wintering grounds with pinpoint accuracy.

children.name: Fulmarus
children.description: Fulmars are sturdy seabirds that belong to the petrel family and are perfectly adapted for life on the open ocean. They have thick, compact bodies with strong wings that allow them to glide effortlessly over rough seas for hours without flapping. These birds spend most of their lives far from land, only coming ashore to nest on rocky coastal cliffs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fulmars can be distinguished from gulls by their distinctive tube-shaped nostrils on top of their thick bills and their stiff-winged gliding flight pattern. Unlike gulls, they rarely flap their wings and instead soar close to the water's surface using wind currents.
children.funFact: When threatened, fulmars can projectile vomit a foul-smelling stomach oil up to several feet away as a defense mechanism, which is how they got their name from the Old Norse words meaning 'foul gull.'

children.description: Shearwaters and petrels are seabirds perfectly adapted for life on the open ocean, spending most of their time flying over waves far from shore. These birds have long, narrow wings that allow them to glide effortlessly just above the water's surface, often appearing to 'shear' through the waves. They come to land only to breed, nesting in burrows or cliff crevices on remote islands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other seabirds, shearwaters and petrels have distinctive tube-shaped nostrils on top of their bills, which help them excrete excess salt from seawater. Their flight style is also unique - they use dynamic soaring, locking their wings and gliding on wind currents with minimal energy expenditure.
children.funFact: Some shearwaters are among the greatest travelers in the animal kingdom, with Sooty Shearwaters making epic figure-8 migrations across the entire Pacific Ocean covering over 40,000 miles annually.

children.name: Oceanitidae
Oceanites
children.description: Oceanites storm-petrels are small seabirds that spend most of their lives flying over the open ocean, only coming to land to breed. They are masters of ocean life, with specialized adaptations that allow them to feed by skimming along the water's surface and even appear to 'walk' on water as they pick up tiny marine creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other storm-petrels, Oceanites species have distinctive white rumps and longer legs that extend beyond their tail in flight. They also have a unique feeding behavior of pattering their feet on the water surface while hovering, which gives them their nickname of 'Mother Carey's chickens.'
children.funFact: Wilson's Storm-Petrel makes one of the longest migrations of any bird, traveling from Antarctic breeding grounds to spend summers in the North Atlantic – a round trip of over 25,000 miles!

children.name: Pelagodroma
children.description: Pelagodroma is a genus containing just one species - the White-faced Storm-Petrel. These small seabirds are true ocean wanderers that spend most of their lives far from shore, only coming to land to breed on remote islands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The White-faced Storm-Petrel is easily recognized by its distinctive white face and forehead, which contrasts sharply with its dark cap and back - a unique pattern among storm-petrels.
children.funFact: White-faced Storm-Petrels have an unusual feeding behavior where they 'patter' across the water's surface with their feet while picking up small fish and plankton, almost appearing to dance on the waves.

children.description: Southern Storm-Petrels are small, tube-nosed seabirds that spend most of their lives flying over the open ocean. These graceful birds are masters of the waves, using their lightweight bodies and long wings to dance across the water's surface as they hunt for tiny fish, plankton, and other marine creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their Northern Storm-Petrel relatives, Southern Storm-Petrels have longer legs and different flight patterns, often pattering their feet on the water surface while feeding. They also have distinctive nostril tube shapes and wing proportions that help scientists tell them apart from other storm-petrel families.
children.funFact: These ocean wanderers can actually "walk on water" by rapidly pattering their webbed feet on the surface while their wings keep them aloft, earning some species the nickname "Jesus birds."

children.name: Hydrobatidae
Hydrobates
children.description: Northern Storm-Petrels are small, dark seabirds that spend most of their lives flying over the open ocean, rarely coming to land except to breed. These agile fliers are known for their distinctive habit of pattering their feet on the water's surface while feeding, appearing to 'walk' on water. They feed primarily on small fish, plankton, and marine invertebrates picked from the ocean surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other storm-petrel groups, Northern Storm-Petrels have deeply forked tails and longer, more pointed wings that give them exceptional maneuverability in flight. They also tend to be slightly larger and have different breeding behaviors compared to their southern relatives.
children.funFact: Storm-petrels got their name from sailors who believed these birds could predict storms, as they often follow ships and appear to increase in numbers before rough weather hits the seas.

children.description: Northern Storm-Petrels are small, dark seabirds that spend most of their lives flying over the open ocean, rarely coming to land except to breed. These tiny oceanic wanderers have a distinctive fluttering flight pattern and can often be seen 'dancing' across the water's surface as they pick up small fish and plankton. They're among the smallest seabirds in the world, yet they're capable of incredible long-distance migrations.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Northern Storm-Petrels are distinguished from other seabirds by their small size, dark plumage, and unique feeding behavior of pattering their feet on the water's surface while flying. They have distinctive tube-shaped nostrils on top of their bills, which help them process salt from seawater.
children.funFact: Storm-petrels got their name from sailors who believed these birds could predict storms - they were often seen following ships during rough weather, actually taking advantage of the easier flying conditions created by wind currents around the vessels.

children.description: Tubenoses are seabirds perfectly adapted for life on the open ocean, spending most of their time far from shore riding wind currents above the waves. They get their name from the distinctive tube-shaped nostrils on top of their bills, which help them process salt water and may enhance their remarkable sense of smell. This group includes everything from tiny storm-petrels that seem to dance on the water's surface to large shearwaters that can glide for miles without flapping their wings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The tubular nostrils on their bills are unique among birds and immediately distinguish tubenoses from all other seabirds. They also have a specialized gland that allows them to drink seawater by filtering out the salt.
children.funFact: Some tubenoses can smell krill and other food sources from over 12 miles away, making them among the few birds that rely heavily on their sense of smell rather than just sight to find food.

children.name: Piciformes
Picidae
Melanerpes
children.description: Melanerpes woodpeckers are medium-sized, boldly colored woodpeckers known for their striking red head markings and distinctive calls. These active birds are often seen clinging to tree trunks and branches, using their strong bills to excavate insects from bark or create nest cavities in dead wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other woodpeckers, Melanerpes species have bright red coloring on their heads and are more social, often seen in small groups. They also have a more varied diet than typical woodpeckers, frequently eating fruits, nuts, and even storing acorns for winter.
children.funFact: Red-headed Woodpeckers are one of the few woodpecker species that actively catch insects in flight, swooping out from perches like flycatchers to snag flying prey.

children.name: Picoides
children.description: Three-toed woodpeckers are specialized birds that have adapted to life in northern coniferous forests. As their name suggests, they have only three toes on each foot instead of the typical four found in most woodpeckers. Both New England species are medium-sized woodpeckers with distinctive black and white plumage patterns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The missing back toe (hallux) sets them apart from all other North American woodpeckers, which have four toes arranged in pairs for gripping tree bark. This three-toed arrangement may actually help them cling more effectively to smooth-barked trees.
children.funFact: These woodpeckers are bark beetle specialists that often follow forest fires and insect outbreaks, feeding on beetle larvae that attack weakened or dead trees.

children.name: Dryobates
children.description: Dryobates woodpeckers are a genus of small to medium-sized woodpeckers known for their black and white plumage patterns. These birds are excellent climbers that use their strong bills to excavate insects from tree bark and create nesting cavities in dead wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dryobates woodpeckers are typically smaller than other woodpecker genera and have distinctive black and white striped or spotted patterns, often with red patches on males' heads.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Dryobates' comes from Greek words meaning 'tree walker,' perfectly describing how these birds spend their lives climbing up and down tree trunks in search of food.

children.name: Colaptes
children.description: Flickers and allies are medium to large woodpeckers known for their ground-foraging behavior and distinctive spotted plumage. Unlike most woodpeckers that primarily feed on tree bark, these birds spend much of their time on the ground hunting for ants and other insects. They have slightly curved bills and strong legs adapted for both climbing trees and hopping on the ground.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Flickers are distinguished from other woodpeckers by their preference for ground feeding and their bold spotted underparts with distinctive crescents or bars. They also have a unique undulating flight pattern and often call from prominent perches rather than while drumming on trees.
children.funFact: Northern Flickers are one of the few woodpecker species that regularly migrate, with northern populations traveling south for winter, and they can live up to 9 years in the wild.

children.name: Dryocopus
children.description: Dryocopus is a genus of large, powerful woodpeckers found across North America, Europe, and Asia. These impressive birds are among the biggest woodpeckers in their respective regions, with strong bills designed for excavating deep into tree trunks and a distinctive undulating flight pattern.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Dryocopus are distinguished from other woodpeckers by their large size, prominent red crests, and preference for excavating rectangular holes rather than round ones when foraging for insects.
children.funFact: The rectangular holes that Dryocopus woodpeckers create while foraging are so distinctive that you can often identify their presence in a forest just by looking at the trees, even if you never see the birds themselves.

children.name: Leuconotopicus
children.description: Leuconotopicus is a genus of medium-sized woodpeckers known for their distinctive black and white plumage patterns. These woodpeckers are expert climbers that use their strong bills to excavate insects from tree bark and create nesting cavities in dead or dying wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their bold black and white striped patterns on the back and wings, with males typically displaying a red patch on the back of their heads that females lack.
children.funFact: The genus name Leuconotopicus literally means 'white-backed woodpecker' in Greek, referring to the prominent white stripe that runs down the middle of their backs.

children.name: Sphyrapicus
children.description: Sapsuckers are specialized woodpeckers that drill neat rows of small holes in tree bark to feed on the sap that flows out. Unlike other woodpeckers that primarily eat insects, these birds have developed a unique feeding strategy that involves maintaining "sap wells" on various tree species. They also eat insects that get trapped in the sticky sap, making them both herbivores and carnivores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sapsuckers can be identified by their habit of drilling distinctive horizontal or vertical rows of small, evenly-spaced holes in tree bark, creating a pattern that looks almost like a grid. Their tongues are shorter and less barbed than other woodpeckers, perfectly adapted for lapping up sap rather than probing deep for insects.
children.funFact: Yellow-bellied Sapsuckers are like tiny tree farmers - they carefully tend their sap wells, returning regularly to maintain them and chase away other animals that try to steal their sweet harvest, including hummingbirds and squirrels.

children.description: Woodpeckers are specialized birds perfectly adapted for life on tree trunks and branches. They have strong, chisel-like beaks for drilling into wood, reinforced skulls to absorb the impact of pecking, and stiff tail feathers that act as a prop while climbing vertically up trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other birds, woodpeckers have zygodactyl feet (two toes facing forward, two backward) for gripping bark, and most species have extremely long tongues that can extend far beyond their beaks to extract insects from deep crevices.
children.funFact: A woodpecker's tongue can be up to four times longer than its beak and wraps around the inside of its skull when not in use!

children.description: Woodpeckers and their allies are specialized birds built for life on tree trunks and branches. Most members of this group have strong, chisel-like beaks for drilling into wood, powerful neck muscles, and stiff tail feathers that act like a kickstand for support while climbing. They use their long, barbed tongues to extract insects, sap, or nuts from crevices in bark.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other birds, most Piciformes have zygodactyl feet with two toes pointing forward and two backward, giving them an excellent grip on vertical surfaces. Their skull structure is specially reinforced to withstand the repeated impact of hammering against wood.
children.funFact: A woodpecker's tongue can extend up to 4 inches beyond its beak tip and wraps around the back of its skull when retracted, stored in a special groove that loops over the top of its head!

children.name: Apodiformes
Trochilidae
Selasphorus
children.description: Selasphorus hummingbirds are small, energetic birds known for their incredible flying abilities and iridescent plumage. These western North American hummingbirds are remarkable long-distance migrants despite their tiny size, with some species traveling thousands of miles between breeding and wintering grounds. They're characterized by their compact bodies, relatively short bills, and the males' brilliant throat patches called gorgets.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other hummingbird genera, Selasphorus species have relatively short, straight bills and are known for their distinctive tail shapes and flight patterns. Males often have colorful, iridescent throat patches and perform elaborate dive displays during courtship that create unique whistling sounds with their tail feathers.
children.funFact: The Rufous Hummingbird has one of the longest migration routes relative to body size of any bird, traveling up to 3,900 miles from Alaska to Mexico - that's 78,470,000 body lengths!

children.name: Archilochus
children.description: Archilochus hummingbirds are small, energetic birds known for their incredible flying abilities and rapid wingbeats. These tiny jewels of the bird world are characterized by their iridescent throat patches (called gorgets) and their ability to hover in place while feeding on nectar from flowers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their relatively small size among hummingbirds and their distinctive gorget patterns - males have brilliant metallic throat patches that can appear ruby red or black depending on the species and lighting angle.
children.funFact: Despite weighing less than a nickel, Ruby-throated Hummingbirds can fly non-stop across the Gulf of Mexico during migration, a journey of over 500 miles!

children.name: Colibri
children.description: Violetears are medium-sized hummingbirds known for the distinctive violet-blue patches of feathers found near their ears, which give them their common name. These energetic birds are primarily found in mountainous regions of Central and South America, where they feed on nectar from flowers and small insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Violetears can be distinguished from other hummingbirds by their metallic violet-blue ear patches and their relatively large size compared to most hummingbird species.
children.funFact: Mexican Violetears are exceptional long-distance travelers and occasionally show up as far north as Canada, making them exciting rare visitors that birders eagerly watch for during migration seasons.

children.name: Cynanthus
children.description: Cynanthus is a small genus of hummingbirds known for their relatively broad, straight bills that help them feed on nectar from flowers. These medium-sized hummingbirds are primarily found in Mexico and Central America, with some species occasionally wandering into the southwestern United States.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their notably wide, flattened bills compared to other hummingbirds, which gives them their common name of 'broad-billed' hummingbirds. Males typically display brilliant metallic blue and green plumage with distinctive coloring patterns.
children.funFact: The Broad-billed Hummingbird's bill is specially adapted to feed on flowers with wide corollas, allowing it to access nectar sources that narrower-billed hummingbirds cannot efficiently exploit.

children.description: Hummingbirds are tiny, jewel-like birds famous for their ability to hover in mid-air and fly backwards. They have incredibly fast wingbeats that create the characteristic humming sound that gives them their name, and they feed primarily on flower nectar using their long, needle-like bills.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hummingbirds are the only birds capable of sustained hovering and backward flight, thanks to their unique wing structure and flight muscles that make up about 30% of their body weight.
children.funFact: A hummingbird's heart beats up to 1,260 times per minute during flight, and they must eat about half their body weight in nectar daily to fuel their high-energy lifestyle.

children.name: Apodidae
Chaetura
children.description: Chaetura swifts are small, dark-colored birds with distinctive cigar-shaped bodies and long, narrow wings built for incredibly fast flight. These aerial specialists spend almost their entire lives in the air, catching insects on the wing and even mating while flying. They have tiny legs and feet that make walking nearly impossible, but their sharp claws are perfect for clinging to vertical surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other swifts, Chaetura swifts have spine-like tips on their tail feathers that help them prop themselves against walls and chimneys when roosting. Their wings are proportionally longer and more curved than those of other swift genera, giving them exceptional maneuverability.
children.funFact: Chimney Swifts can't perch on branches like other birds - they must cling to vertical surfaces, and when they sleep, they hang vertically against walls with their tail spines acting like a built-in kickstand.

children.description: Swifts are small, fast-flying birds that spend almost their entire lives in the air, only landing to nest and roost. They have extremely long, narrow wings and short legs that make them perfectly adapted for aerial life. These insect-eating birds can be seen darting through the sky at incredible speeds, catching their prey on the wing.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Swifts can be distinguished from swallows by their longer, more curved wings that form a crescent or boomerang shape in flight, and their inability to perch on wires or branches due to their tiny, weak feet.
children.funFact: Swifts are among the fastest flying birds in level flight, and some species can even sleep while flying by shutting down half their brain at a time.

children.description: Swifts and hummingbirds are two families of birds that share remarkably similar wing structures and flight capabilities, despite looking quite different. Both groups have exceptionally strong flight muscles and can hover, fly backwards, and perform aerial acrobatics that few other birds can match. They spend most of their lives in the air, with swifts catching insects on the wing and hummingbirds hovering at flowers to drink nectar.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These birds have uniquely structured wings with very short arm bones but extremely long hand bones, creating wings that are mostly 'hand' rather than 'arm.' This wing design, along with their powerful flight muscles, gives them unmatched maneuverability and the ability to beat their wings at incredible speeds.
children.funFact: Hummingbirds can beat their wings up to 80 times per second, while some swifts can sleep while flying, shutting down half their brain at a time during long migrations.

children.name: Suliformes
Phalacrocoracidae
Nannopterum
children.description: American Cormorants are large, dark waterbirds that are expert divers and fishers. They have long, flexible necks, hooked bills perfect for catching fish, and webbed feet that make them strong swimmers both on the surface and underwater.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other cormorant groups, American Cormorants have distinctive throat pouches that can be colorful during breeding season, and they're found primarily in the Americas rather than other continents.
children.funFact: These cormorants have unusually wettable feathers compared to other waterbirds, which helps them dive deeper but means they must spread their wings to dry after swimming - a classic pose you'll often see them striking on docks and rocks.

children.name: Phalacrocorax
children.description: Typical Old World Cormorants are large, dark waterbirds that are expert divers and fishers. They have long, hook-tipped bills perfect for catching fish underwater, and their webbed feet make them powerful swimmers. These birds are often seen perched on rocks or posts with their wings spread wide to dry their feathers after diving.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other cormorant groups, typical Old World cormorants are generally larger and more robust, with the Great Cormorant being one of the largest cormorant species in the world. They also tend to have more prominent throat pouches and longer, more substantial bills than their relatives.
children.funFact: Great Cormorants have been used by fishermen in Asia for over 1,000 years - the birds dive to catch fish but wear special collars that prevent them from swallowing their catch, allowing the fishermen to retrieve it.

children.description: Cormorants and shags are large, dark waterbirds that are expert fishers, diving underwater to catch fish with their sharp, hooked beaks. These sleek birds have webbed feet for swimming and long, flexible necks that help them strike at prey beneath the surface. After fishing, you'll often see them perched with their wings spread wide to dry their feathers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike ducks and other waterbirds, cormorants have less waterproof feathers that become waterlogged, allowing them to dive deeper and swim more efficiently underwater. Their throat pouch and distinctive fishing behavior also set them apart from similar-looking birds.
children.funFact: Cormorants have been trained by fishermen in some parts of the world for over 1,000 years, with rings placed around their necks to prevent them from swallowing the largest fish they catch.

children.name: Sulidae
Morus
children.description: Gannets are large seabirds known for their spectacular high-speed dives into the ocean to catch fish. These powerful birds have streamlined bodies, long pointed wings, and dagger-like bills perfectly adapted for their plunge-diving lifestyle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Gannets are distinguished from other seabirds by their distinctive torpedo-shaped bodies, forward-facing eyes for better depth perception, and their unique habit of diving from heights of 30-100 feet into the water.
children.funFact: Northern Gannets can reach speeds of up to 60 mph when diving and have special air sacs in their heads and chests that act like bubble wrap to cushion the impact when they hit the water.

children.name: Sula
children.description: Typical boobies are large seabirds known for their spectacular diving abilities, plunging headfirst into the ocean from great heights to catch fish. These powerful fliers have streamlined bodies, long pointed wings, and sharp beaks perfectly adapted for their marine lifestyle. They're social birds that often feed in flocks and nest in colonies on coastal cliffs or islands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other seabirds, boobies have forward-facing eyes that provide excellent depth perception for precision diving, and their nostrils are sealed shut to prevent water from entering during high-speed plunges into the sea.
children.funFact: Boobies can dive from heights of up to 80 feet and hit the water at speeds of 60 mph, with special air sacs in their necks and chests that act like built-in airbags to cushion the impact!

children.description: Boobies and gannets are large seabirds built for spectacular diving into the ocean to catch fish. They have streamlined bodies, long pointed wings, and sharp bills that help them plunge from great heights into the water at speeds up to 60 mph. These birds are excellent flyers and spend most of their time soaring over coastal waters and the open sea.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other seabirds, boobies and gannets have forward-facing eyes that give them binocular vision for judging distances when diving, and their nostrils are sealed to prevent water from entering during high-speed plunges. They also have distinctive long, dagger-like bills and webbed feet with all four toes connected.
children.funFact: Northern Gannets have built-in shock absorbers in their necks and reinforced skulls that allow them to dive from heights of up to 100 feet without injury, hitting the water like living missiles to catch fish below the surface.

children.name: Anhingidae
Anhinga
children.description: Darters are large waterbirds known for their distinctive swimming behavior - they swim with only their snake-like head and neck visible above water, earning them the nickname 'snakebird.' These skilled underwater hunters use their sharp, pointed bills to spear fish and other aquatic prey. They have dense bones and reduced air sacs that help them dive and swim underwater with remarkable agility.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other waterbirds, darters lack waterproof feathers and must spread their wings to dry after swimming. Their long, thin neck has a unique kink that allows them to strike prey like a spear by rapidly straightening it underwater.
children.funFact: Darters are one of the few birds that can control their buoyancy - they can partially submerge their body while keeping their head above water, or sink completely below the surface to hunt.

children.description: Darters are large, long-necked waterbirds that are expert underwater hunters. They have sharp, pointed bills and swim with their bodies submerged, often with only their snake-like necks visible above water. These birds are found in freshwater environments like swamps, ponds, and slow-moving rivers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other waterbirds, darters have less waterproof feathers that help them sink and swim underwater more easily. They must frequently spread their wings to dry after swimming, creating their characteristic pose with outstretched wings.
children.funFact: Darters are sometimes called 'snakebirds' because when swimming, only their long, curved necks are visible above water, making them look like swimming snakes.

children.name: Fregatidae
Fregata
children.description: Frigatebirds are large, distinctive seabirds with extremely long, narrow wings and deeply forked tails that make them unmistakable in flight. They are skilled aerial pirates, often harassing other seabirds to force them to regurgitate their catch, which the frigatebirds then steal mid-air. These tropical and subtropical birds are perfectly adapted for a life spent mostly soaring over warm ocean waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Frigatebirds have the largest wing-to-body-weight ratio of any bird, allowing them to soar effortlessly for hours without flapping. Males are famous for their bright red throat pouches that they inflate like balloons during courtship displays.
children.funFact: Despite being seabirds, frigatebirds have very little waterproofing in their feathers and will actually sink if they land on the water, so they must catch all their food from the surface or steal it from other birds.

children.description: Frigatebirds are large seabirds known for their impressive soaring abilities and piratical behavior on the ocean. These tropical and subtropical birds have extremely long, narrow wings and deeply forked tails that make them masters of flight over warm coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Frigatebirds have the largest wing-to-body-weight ratio of any bird, allowing them to soar for weeks without landing. Males are famous for their bright red throat pouches that they inflate like balloons during courtship displays.
children.funFact: Frigatebirds are expert thieves that harass other seabirds in flight, forcing them to regurgitate their catch so the frigatebirds can snatch the food mid-air—a behavior called kleptoparasitism.

children.description: Gannets, cormorants, and their allies are skilled diving seabirds that spend most of their lives hunting fish in marine waters. These birds share a unique feature where all four toes are connected by webbing, unlike most other birds that only have webbing between three front toes. They're perfectly adapted for underwater pursuit of fish, with streamlined bodies and waterproof feathers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets this group apart is their distinctive four-webbed-toe foot structure and their specialized diving abilities. Most members can dive from great heights or swim underwater to catch fish, with some species able to plunge from over 100 feet above the water's surface.
children.funFact: Northern Gannets have forward-facing eyes and special air sacs in their heads and necks that act like built-in airbags, cushioning the impact when they dive-bomb into the ocean at speeds up to 60 mph!

children.name: Falconiformes
Falconidae
Falco
children.description: Typical falcons are sleek, powerful raptors known for their incredible speed and agility in flight. These birds of prey have streamlined bodies, pointed wings, and sharp talons that make them expert hunters of other birds and small animals. All members of this genus share similar body shapes and hunting techniques, though they vary considerably in size from the tiny American Kestrel to the massive Gyrfalcon.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other raptors, typical falcons have a distinctive notched upper bill called a 'tomial tooth' that helps them quickly kill prey by severing the spinal cord. They also tend to catch prey in dramatic high-speed dives rather than from perches like hawks and eagles.
children.funFact: The Peregrine Falcon holds the world record as the fastest animal on Earth, reaching speeds over 240 mph during hunting dives!

children.name: Caracara
children.description: Crested Caracaras are large, distinctive birds of prey that belong to the falcon family but behave more like vultures. They are opportunistic feeders that spend much of their time walking on the ground, scavenging for carrion, insects, and small animals rather than hunting from the air like most raptors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical falcons, Crested Caracaras have long legs adapted for ground walking, a prominent crest of feathers on their heads, and distinctive black and white plumage with bright orange facial skin.
children.funFact: Crested Caracaras are sometimes called "Mexican Eagles" and actually appear on Mexico's flag and coat of arms, despite being more closely related to falcons than true eagles.

children.description: Falcons and caracaras are powerful birds of prey known for their incredible speed and hunting prowess. They have sharp, hooked beaks with a distinctive notch called a 'tomial tooth' that helps them deliver a quick, fatal bite to their prey. These raptors are found worldwide and include some of the fastest animals on Earth.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other raptors, falcons kill their prey primarily with their beaks rather than their talons. They also have longer, more pointed wings than hawks and eagles, making them built for speed rather than soaring.
children.funFact: Peregrine falcons are the fastest animals in the world, reaching speeds over 240 mph when diving to catch prey.

children.description: Falcons and caracaras are powerful birds of prey known for their incredible speed and hunting prowess. They have sharp, hooked beaks, strong talons, and exceptional eyesight that helps them spot prey from great distances. These raptors are found worldwide and range from the lightning-fast peregrine falcon to the more ground-dwelling caracaras.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other raptors, falcons have a distinctive tooth-like projection on their upper beak called a tomial tooth, which they use to deliver a quick, fatal bite to their prey's neck. They also have pointed wings built for speed rather than soaring.
children.funFact: Peregrine falcons are the fastest animals on Earth, reaching speeds over 240 mph during their hunting dives!

children.name: Columbiformes
Columbidae
Zenaida
children.description: Zenaida doves are medium-sized, graceful doves known for their soft, mournful calls and elegant flight patterns. These doves share similar body shapes with relatively long, pointed tails and streamlined builds that make them excellent fliers. They're ground-foraging birds that primarily eat seeds and are commonly seen in both rural and suburban areas throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Zenaida doves can be distinguished from other dove groups by their pointed tails, relatively slender builds, and distinctive soft cooing calls. They also have small, dark spots on their wings and tend to be more graceful in flight than the stockier rock doves (pigeons).
children.funFact: The genus Zenaida was named after Princess Zénaïde Bonaparte, the niece of Napoleon Bonaparte, who was married to a prominent ornithologist in the early 1800s.

children.name: Streptopelia
children.description: Turtle-doves and collared-doves are medium-sized pigeons known for their gentle cooing calls and distinctive dark collar markings around their necks. These graceful birds have soft, muted plumage in shades of gray, brown, and pink, and are often seen perching on power lines or foraging on the ground for seeds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other pigeons, members of this genus have a prominent dark partial collar or band across the back and sides of their neck. They also tend to be more slender and elegant in build compared to the stockier rock pigeons commonly seen in cities.
children.funFact: The Eurasian Collared-Dove has one of the most remarkable range expansions in bird history, spreading from Asia across all of Europe and into North America in just the past century.

children.name: Columba
children.description: Typical Old World Pigeons are medium to large-sized pigeons that originally come from Europe, Asia, and Africa. These sturdy birds are characterized by their compact bodies, small heads, and strong flying abilities. They're well-adapted to both wild rocky habitats and urban environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other pigeon groups, Columba pigeons tend to be larger and more robust, with relatively plain coloration dominated by grays, browns, and whites rather than bright tropical colors.
children.funFact: The Rock Pigeon was one of the first birds ever domesticated by humans over 5,000 years ago, originally bred for food and message delivery before becoming the familiar city pigeon we see today.

children.name: Columbina
children.description: Small Ground Doves are tiny, compact doves that spend most of their time walking and foraging on the ground rather than perching in trees. These diminutive birds are among the smallest members of the dove family, with short tails and legs perfectly adapted for terrestrial life. They prefer open habitats like fields, roadsides, and garden areas where they can easily search for seeds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These doves are much smaller than other North American doves and have a distinctive ground-hugging behavior, rarely flying high or far when disturbed. Their short, rounded wings produce a distinctive whirring sound during their brief, low flights.
children.funFact: When startled, Common Ground Doves typically run along the ground like tiny quail before taking flight, and they can actually run faster than many people expect for such small birds.

children.description: Pigeons and doves are medium-sized birds with compact bodies, small heads, and gentle dispositions that are found in both urban and natural environments. They're known for their soft cooing calls and their ability to produce a nutritious substance called 'crop milk' to feed their young. These birds are excellent fliers with strong wing muscles, though they spend much of their time walking on the ground searching for seeds and fruits.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other seed-eating birds, pigeons and doves can drink water by suction without tilting their heads back, and they're unique among birds in producing crop milk for their chicks. They also have a distinctive head-bobbing walk and tend to build simple, flimsy nests made of twigs.
children.funFact: The famous homing pigeons can navigate back to their roosts from hundreds of miles away using a combination of magnetic fields, the sun's position, and even low-frequency sound waves that humans can't hear.

children.description: Pigeons and doves are seed-eating birds known for their gentle cooing calls and smooth, graceful flight. They have compact bodies, small heads, and the unique ability to drink water by sucking it up rather than tilting their heads back like most birds. These birds are found worldwide and are especially common in urban areas where they've adapted well to city life.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other birds, pigeons and doves produce a nutritious "crop milk" to feed their young, similar to how mammals produce milk. They also have a distinctive nodding head motion when walking and can rotate their heads nearly 340 degrees.
children.funFact: Pigeons have incredible navigation abilities and can find their way home from over 1,000 miles away using the Earth's magnetic field, the sun's position, and even infrasound from ocean waves.

children.name: Podicipediformes
Podicipedidae
Podiceps
children.description: Typical grebes are medium-sized diving waterbirds with sleek, streamlined bodies perfectly adapted for underwater hunting. They have pointed bills, compact wings, and legs positioned far back on their bodies, making them excellent swimmers but awkward on land. These birds are known for their elaborate courtship displays and their ability to dive completely underwater to catch fish and aquatic invertebrates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other grebe groups, typical grebes are characterized by their medium size and distinctive breeding plumages that often feature colorful head ornaments like horns, crests, or ear tufts. They also have more pointed bills compared to the broader bills of larger grebes.
children.funFact: Typical grebes actually eat their own feathers and feed them to their chicks, which helps protect their stomachs from sharp fish bones and may aid in digestion by forming pellets that can be regurgitated.

children.name: Aechmophorus
children.description: The genus Aechmophorus contains two nearly identical species of large, elegant waterbirds known for their striking black and white plumage and long, slender necks. These grebes are famous for their elaborate courtship displays, including synchronized dancing and running across the water surface together. Both species are excellent divers that hunt for fish in freshwater lakes and coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Western and Clark's Grebes are distinguished from other grebes by their large size, dramatic black-and-white coloration, and exceptionally long necks. The two species in this genus are so similar that they were once considered the same species, differing mainly in bill color and the extent of black markings around the eye.
children.funFact: These grebes perform one of nature's most spectacular courtship rituals called 'rushing,' where pairs run side-by-side across the water surface for up to 60 feet, their bodies held vertically and necks arched gracefully.

children.name: Podilymbus
children.description: Podilymbus grebes are small, compact waterbirds with thick, chicken-like bills that are perfectly adapted for crushing their prey. These diving birds are excellent swimmers that can control their buoyancy by compressing their feathers to trap less air, allowing them to sink gradually into the water or float at different levels.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other grebes with thin, pointed bills, Podilymbus grebes have distinctively thick, blunt bills that are ideal for grabbing and crushing crayfish, insects, and small fish rather than spearing them.
children.funFact: Pied-billed Grebes are sometimes called 'hell-divers' because they can disappear underwater so quickly and completely when startled that early observers thought they had vanished into thin air.

children.description: Grebes are specialized diving waterbirds perfectly adapted for life in lakes, ponds, and coastal waters. They have streamlined bodies, lobed toes instead of webbed feet, and legs positioned far back on their bodies for powerful underwater propulsion. These expert swimmers and divers feed primarily on fish, aquatic insects, and small crustaceans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike ducks and other waterbirds, grebes have unique lobed toes rather than webbed feet, and their legs are positioned so far back that they can barely walk on land. They also have the remarkable ability to control their buoyancy by compressing their feathers to sink quietly beneath the surface.
children.funFact: Grebes eat their own feathers and feed them to their chicks, which helps form a plug in their stomachs that filters out fish bones and other indigestible items before they reach the intestines.

children.description: Grebes are specialized diving birds perfectly adapted for life on the water. They have streamlined bodies, lobed toes instead of webbed feet, and legs positioned far back on their bodies for powerful underwater propulsion. These aquatic birds are excellent swimmers and divers, spending most of their time on lakes, ponds, and coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike ducks and other waterfowl, grebes have distinctive lobed toes rather than webbed feet, and their legs are positioned so far back that they can barely walk on land. They also have the unique ability to control their buoyancy by compressing their feathers and expelling air from their bodies.
children.funFact: Grebes eat their own feathers and feed them to their chicks, which helps protect their stomachs from sharp fish bones and forms pellets that aid in digestion.

children.name: Psittaciformes
Psittacidae
Myiopsitta
children.description: Monk and Cliff Parakeets are small, stocky parrots known for their bright green plumage and social nature. These South American natives are unique among parrots for building large, communal stick nests rather than nesting in tree cavities. They are highly adaptable birds that can survive in cooler climates than most other parrot species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other parrots, Myiopsitta parakeets construct elaborate communal nests made of twigs and branches, often in trees or on man-made structures. They also have distinctive gray faces and breasts that contrast with their bright green wings and backs.
children.funFact: Monk Parakeets are the only parrot species that builds stick nests - all other parrots nest in cavities, and their massive communal nests can weigh over 200 pounds and house multiple families.

children.name: Amazona
children.description: Amazon parrots are medium to large-sized, stocky parrots known for their vibrant green plumage and remarkable intelligence. These social birds are native to Central and South America, where they live in flocks and feed primarily on fruits, seeds, and nuts. They are excellent mimics and can live for many decades, making them popular but challenging pets.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Amazon parrots are distinguished from other parrots by their predominantly green coloration with colorful markings on their heads, necks, or wings, and their robust, compact build. They have short, square tails and strong, thick beaks perfectly adapted for cracking tough seeds and nuts.
children.funFact: Amazon parrots are known for their "pinning" behavior - when excited, their pupils rapidly contract and dilate, making their eyes appear to flash, which is often accompanied by fanned tail feathers and raised head feathers.

children.name: Aratinga
children.description: Aratinga parakeets are medium-sized, colorful parrots native to Central and South America. They are known for their vibrant green plumage often accented with bright yellows, oranges, or reds on their heads and wings. These social birds typically travel in flocks and are quite vocal, using a variety of calls to communicate.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Aratinga parakeets can be distinguished from other parakeet genera by their relatively large size, long pointed tails, and distinctive bright head coloration patterns. They also have particularly strong, loud calls that carry over long distances.
children.funFact: Golden-capped Parakeets are excellent mimics and can learn to imitate human speech as well as the calls of other bird species in their environment.

children.description: The New World and African Parrots are a large family of colorful, intelligent birds known for their strong, curved beaks and zygodactyl feet (two toes pointing forward, two backward). These highly social parrots are excellent climbers and many species are capable of mimicking human speech and other sounds. They primarily feed on seeds, fruits, and nuts, using their powerful beaks to crack open tough shells.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This family is distinguished from other parrot groups by their geographic distribution across the Americas and Africa, and their generally larger size compared to other parrot families. Unlike Old World parrots, many species in this family show exceptional vocal learning abilities and complex social behaviors.
children.funFact: Amazon parrots can live over 80 years in captivity and have been observed using tools in the wild, such as using sticks to scratch themselves in hard-to-reach places.

children.name: Psittaculidae
Melopsittacus
children.description: Budgerigars are small, colorful parrots native to Australia that have become one of the world's most popular pet birds. They are highly social birds that naturally live in large flocks and are known for their ability to mimic sounds and learn simple words. In New England, budgerigars are found as escaped or released pet birds rather than as native wildlife.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Budgerigars can be distinguished from other small parrots by their distinctive black barring on yellow-green wings and backs, bright yellow heads, and small size of about 7 inches long. Their natural wild coloration is primarily green and yellow, though captive breeding has produced many color variations.
children.funFact: Budgerigars have been kept as pets for over 160 years, and a budgie named Puck holds the world record for the largest vocabulary of any bird, knowing over 1,700 words!

children.name: Agapornis
children.description: Lovebirds are small, colorful parrots known for their strong pair bonds and affectionate behavior toward their mates. These compact birds have short, blunt tails and powerful beaks perfect for cracking seeds and nuts. They are native to Africa and Madagascar, though some species have established populations elsewhere through escapes or releases.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lovebirds are smaller than most other parrots and have distinctively short, square-shaped tails rather than long, pointed ones. Their strong pair-bonding behavior and tendency to sit closely together sets them apart from more solitary parrot species.
children.funFact: Lovebirds got their name because mated pairs spend hours sitting side by side, preening each other's feathers and appearing to 'kiss' - though they're actually regurgitating food to share with their partner!

children.description: Old World Parrots are a diverse family of colorful, intelligent birds originally from Africa, Asia, and Australia. They have strong, curved beaks perfect for cracking seeds and nuts, along with zygodactyl feet (two toes forward, two backward) that help them climb and manipulate food. These social birds are known for their problem-solving abilities and complex vocalizations.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike New World parrots, Old World parrots lack the waxy cere (the area around the nostrils) and tend to have more subdued coloration, though many species are still brilliantly colored. They also have different skull structures and feeding adaptations compared to their New World relatives.
children.funFact: Budgerigars can see ultraviolet light, revealing hidden patterns on their feathers that are invisible to human eyes but help them recognize each other and assess potential mates.

children.name: Cacatuidae
Nymphicus
children.description: Cockatiels are small, crested parrots native to Australia that have become one of the most popular pet birds worldwide. They are characterized by their distinctive feathered crest that can be raised or lowered to express their mood, and their long, pointed tail feathers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other parrots, cockatiels have a prominent crest of feathers on their heads and are typically gray with bright orange or yellow patches on their cheeks. They are also smaller and more slender than most other parrot species.
children.funFact: Cockatiels can live over 20 years and are excellent whistlers, often learning to mimic household sounds like smoke alarms, microwaves, and telephone rings better than human speech.

children.description: Cockatoos are distinctive parrots known for their prominent feathered crests that can be raised or lowered to express emotions and communicate. These intelligent birds are native to Australia and nearby regions, with strong beaks perfect for cracking seeds and nuts. They're highly social creatures that form strong bonds with their flocks and are known for their playful, curious nature.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other parrots, cockatoos have moveable head crests and tend to be predominantly white, gray, or black in coloration rather than the bright greens and reds typical of many parrot families. They also lack the oil gland that gives other parrots their vibrant colors, instead producing a fine powder that helps keep their feathers clean.
children.funFact: Cockatoos can live over 100 years in some cases, and they're among the few animals that have been observed making and using tools in the wild, such as using sticks to extract insects from tree bark.

children.description: Parrots are colorful, intelligent birds known for their curved beaks, zygodactyl feet (two toes forward, two backward), and remarkable ability to mimic sounds. They range from tiny budgerigars to large macaws, and are found naturally in tropical and subtropical regions around the world. Most species are highly social and feed primarily on seeds, fruits, and nuts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Parrots have distinctively curved, hooked beaks that are perfectly adapted for cracking seeds and nuts, along with their unique foot structure that allows them to grasp objects like hands. Their exceptional vocal abilities and problem-solving intelligence set them apart from other bird orders.
children.funFact: Some parrot species can live over 100 years, and they're among the few animals that can learn to use words in context rather than just mimicking sounds.

children.name: Gaviiformes
Gaviidae
Gavia
children.description: Loons are large aquatic birds perfectly adapted for life on northern lakes and coastal waters. All members of this genus share a streamlined body, webbed feet positioned far back on their bodies, and dense bones that help them dive underwater to catch fish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other waterbirds, loons have solid bones rather than hollow ones, making them excellent divers but requiring them to run across the water's surface to take flight. Their legs are positioned so far back that they can barely walk on land, earning them their name from the Old Norse word 'lomr' meaning lame.
children.funFact: Loons can dive up to 200 feet deep and stay underwater for up to 5 minutes while hunting, using their dagger-like bills to spear fish and swallow them headfirst.

children.description: Loons are large, diving waterbirds perfectly adapted for life on northern lakes and coastal waters. These sleek birds have solid bones (unlike most birds which have hollow bones) that help them dive deep underwater to catch fish, and their legs are positioned far back on their bodies for powerful swimming.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Loons can be distinguished from other waterbirds by their dagger-like bills, distinctive spotted or striped plumage patterns, and their haunting, wailing calls that echo across northern lakes.
children.funFact: Loons are so specialized for swimming that they can barely walk on land - their legs are positioned so far back that they must push themselves along on their bellies when moving across the ground to their nests.

children.description: Loons are distinctive aquatic birds perfectly adapted for life on northern lakes and coastal waters. All members of this order share a streamlined body design, webbed feet positioned far back on their bodies, and dense bones that help them dive underwater to catch fish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other water birds, loons have solid bones rather than hollow ones, making them excellent divers but requiring them to run across the water surface to become airborne.
children.funFact: Loons are famous for their haunting, wailing calls that can carry for miles across a quiet lake - each individual has a unique voice that their family members can recognize.

children.name: Caprimulgiformes
Caprimulgidae
Antrostomus
children.description: Typical American nightjars are nocturnal birds with incredibly cryptic plumage that makes them nearly invisible when resting on the forest floor during the day. These medium-sized birds have large eyes adapted for night vision, tiny bills but enormous mouths for catching insects in flight, and soft feathers that allow them to fly silently through the woods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other nightjar groups, Antrostomus species are known for their distinctive, repetitive calls that sound like spoken phrases - giving them their common names like "whip-poor-will" and "chuck-will's-widow."
children.funFact: These birds are so well-camouflaged that they often remain motionless even when approached closely, relying on their bark-like plumage pattern rather than flying away to avoid detection.

children.name: Chordeiles
children.description: Typical nighthawks are medium-sized birds that are active during dawn and dusk, spending their days resting motionless on the ground or tree branches. They have large mouths and excellent flying abilities, catching insects while soaring through the air. These birds are known for their distinctive diving displays and booming calls during breeding season.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other nightjar family members, typical nighthawks have longer, more pointed wings and prefer open habitats over dense forests. They also have white wing patches that flash conspicuously during flight.
children.funFact: Despite their name, nighthawks aren't actually hawks at all - they're more closely related to hummingbirds and swifts, and their scientific name Chordeiles means 'evening harp' referring to the musical sound their wings make during courtship dives.

children.description: Nightjars and their allies are nocturnal birds with cryptic, mottled plumage that provides excellent camouflage against tree bark, leaves, and ground cover. They have large eyes adapted for night vision, wide gaping mouths for catching insects in flight, and soft, silent flight feathers. These birds spend their days resting motionless on the ground or perched lengthwise on branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other aerial insectivores, nightjars have tiny bills but enormous mouths that open incredibly wide, surrounded by bristles that help funnel flying insects. Their eyes are proportionally much larger than similar-sized birds, and their flight is distinctively silent and moth-like.
children.funFact: Common Nighthawks aren't actually hawks at all - they got their name because they're often seen hunting insects at dusk when hawks are also active, but they're more closely related to hummingbirds than to any raptor!

children.description: Nightjars and their allies are nocturnal birds perfectly adapted for hunting insects in the dark. These medium-sized birds have incredibly wide mouths that open like nets to catch flying insects, along with soft, mottled plumage that provides excellent camouflage during the day when they rest on the ground or tree branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other birds, nightjars have tiny bills but enormous gapes that can open wider than their heads, plus specialized bristles around their mouths to help funnel insects in. Their eyes are also exceptionally large for their body size to maximize light gathering in dim conditions.
children.funFact: Common Nighthawks aren't actually hawks at all, and despite their name, they often hunt during daylight hours, performing dramatic diving displays where their wing feathers create a distinctive booming sound.

children.name: Cuculiformes
Cuculidae
Coccyzus
children.description: Coccyzus cuckoos are sleek, long-tailed birds that prefer to stay hidden in dense woodland canopy. These secretive birds are more often heard than seen, known for their distinctive calls that echo through the forest. They are skilled insect hunters, particularly fond of caterpillars that other birds avoid.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their Old World relatives, Coccyzus cuckoos don't lay their eggs in other birds' nests - they build their own shallow, flimsy nests. They can be distinguished from other similar birds by their curved bills, long graduated tails with white spots underneath, and their habit of moving slowly and deliberately through branches.
children.funFact: Yellow-billed Cuckoos are sometimes called 'rain crows' because their calls often increase before storms, and they're one of the few birds that can safely eat fuzzy caterpillars like tent caterpillars that are toxic to most other species.

children.name: Cuculus
children.description: Typical Old World Cuckoos are medium-sized birds known for their distinctive calls and secretive behavior. Most species in this group are brood parasites, meaning they lay their eggs in other birds' nests and let the host parents raise their young. They have long, pointed wings and long tails that help them fly swiftly through forests and woodlands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These cuckoos are distinguished from New World cuckoos by their parasitic breeding behavior and their characteristic two-note calls. They have more slender builds and longer wings compared to their American cousins, which typically build their own nests.
children.funFact: The Common Cuckoo's famous 'cuckoo' call is actually made only by males during breeding season - females make a distinctive bubbling trill sound instead!

children.description: Cuckoos are medium-sized birds known for their distinctive calls and secretive nature. Most species have slender bodies, long tails, and curved bills that help them catch insects and caterpillars that other birds avoid. They're often heard more than seen, preferring to stay hidden in dense foliage.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cuckoos have a unique foot structure called zygodactyl, with two toes pointing forward and two backward, which helps them grip branches while moving through trees. Unlike most songbirds, they have a more direct, undulating flight pattern.
children.funFact: While European cuckoos are famous for laying their eggs in other birds' nests, New England's cuckoos actually build their own nests and raise their own young, though they're such devoted parents that they'll sometimes adopt orphaned chicks from other species.

children.description: Cuckoos are medium-sized birds known for their distinctive calls and fascinating breeding behaviors. Most species have long tails, slightly curved bills, and zygodactyl feet (two toes pointing forward, two backward) that help them grip branches while moving through dense vegetation. They are primarily insectivores, with many species specializing in eating caterpillars that other birds avoid.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cuckoos are most famous for their brood parasitism - many species lay their eggs in other birds' nests and let the host parents raise their young. Their unique foot structure and sleek, streamlined body shape also set them apart from other bird orders.
children.funFact: Some cuckoo chicks are so aggressive that they will push the host bird's own eggs and babies out of the nest, ensuring they receive all the parental care for themselves!

children.name: Cathartiformes
Cathartidae
Cathartes
children.description: Cathartes vultures are large soaring birds known for their exceptional ability to locate carrion using their keen sense of smell. These New World vultures have bare, featherless heads and necks that help keep them clean while feeding on dead animals. They play a crucial ecological role as nature's cleanup crew, preventing the spread of disease by consuming decomposing matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other vultures, Cathartes species have well-developed nostrils and rely heavily on their sense of smell to find food, rather than just using their eyesight. They also have a distinctive two-toned underwing pattern visible during flight.
children.funFact: Turkey vultures have such a powerful sense of smell that gas companies sometimes add the scent of carrion to natural gas pipelines - when the birds circle overhead, it helps workers locate gas leaks!

children.name: Coragyps
children.description: Coragyps is a genus containing only one living species - the Black Vulture. These are large, dark-colored scavenging birds with broad wings designed for soaring on thermal air currents as they search for carrion.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike Turkey Vultures, Black Vultures have shorter, broader wings with distinctive white patches near the wingtips, and they hold their wings flat while soaring rather than in a V-shape.
children.funFact: Black Vultures are highly social birds that often roost and feed in groups, and they have been observed following Turkey Vultures to food sources since Turkey Vultures have a superior sense of smell.

children.description: New World Vultures are large scavenging birds that feed primarily on carrion (dead animals). They have bare heads and necks, powerful beaks for tearing flesh, and excellent eyesight for spotting food from great distances. These important cleanup crew members soar effortlessly on thermal air currents while searching for their next meal.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike Old World vultures found in Africa and Asia, New World vultures have a highly developed sense of smell that helps them locate decaying animals. They also lack the strong grasping talons of raptors, having feet better suited for walking than catching prey.
children.funFact: Turkey Vultures can smell a dead mouse from over a mile away, making them so good at finding gas leaks that utility companies sometimes follow circling vultures to locate pipeline problems!

children.description: New World vultures are large scavenging birds that feed primarily on carrion (dead animals). They have broad wings perfect for soaring on thermal air currents as they search for food across vast territories. These impressive birds play a crucial ecological role as nature's cleanup crew, helping prevent the spread of disease by consuming dead animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike Old World vultures found in Africa and Asia, New World vultures have an exceptional sense of smell that helps them locate carrion from great distances. They also lack the strong grasping talons of raptors, instead having feet better suited for walking on the ground.
children.funFact: Turkey vultures can smell a dead mouse from over a mile away, making them one of the few bird species with such a highly developed sense of smell.

children.name: Coraciiformes
Alcedinidae
Megaceryle
children.description: Large Crested Kingfishers are robust, fish-eating birds with prominent crests and powerful bills designed for catching aquatic prey. These birds are typically found near water bodies where they hunt by diving headfirst from perches or while hovering above the water. They excavate tunnel nests in earthen banks along rivers, lakes, and coastlines.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This group stands out from other kingfishers by their larger size, more pronounced crests, and distinctive rattling calls. They are also among the few kingfisher species that can handle larger fish prey due to their robust build and powerful bills.
children.funFact: Belted Kingfishers are one of the few bird species where females are more colorful than males - female Belted Kingfishers sport an additional rusty belt across their belly that males lack.

children.description: Kingfishers are compact, sturdy birds known for their fishing abilities and distinctive appearance. They have large heads, long straight bills, and relatively short legs, with most species sporting vibrant blue and white plumage. These birds are expert hunters that dive headfirst into water to catch fish, though some species also eat insects and small animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Kingfishers can be identified by their oversized heads relative to their body size, dagger-like bills, and their unique hunting style of diving from perches into water. Their feet are syndactyl, meaning some toes are fused together, which helps distinguish them from other waterbirds.
children.funFact: Kingfishers nest in tunnels they excavate in riverbanks, sometimes digging burrows up to 3 feet deep that end in a chamber where they raise their young.

children.description: Rollers, kingfishers, and their allies are a diverse group of colorful birds known for their impressive hunting abilities and unique nesting habits. Most members of this order have large heads, strong bills, and excellent eyesight that helps them spot prey from a distance. They're found worldwide in various habitats, from tropical forests to wetlands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These birds are characterized by their syndactyl feet, where some toes are fused together, and their tendency to nest in cavities they excavate themselves. Many species have brilliantly colored plumage with iridescent blues, greens, and other vibrant hues.
children.funFact: Kingfishers can adjust their vision to account for light refraction in water, allowing them to accurately judge where fish actually are beneath the surface when diving for prey.

children.name: Phoenicopteriformes
Phoenicopteridae
Phoenicopterus
children.description: Large Flamingos are the tallest and most robust members of the flamingo family, known for their impressive size and distinctive pink coloration. These wading birds have long, curved necks, stilts-like legs, and specialized curved bills perfectly adapted for filter-feeding in shallow waters. They are highly social birds that gather in large flocks and are famous for their synchronized group behaviors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Large Flamingos are distinguished from other flamingo species by their greater height (up to 5 feet tall) and more intense pink-red coloration. Their bills have a more pronounced downward curve and black tip compared to smaller flamingo species.
children.funFact: Large Flamingos can only bend their knees backwards and often stand on one leg to conserve body heat, tucking the other leg up into their warm belly feathers.

children.description: Flamingos are large wading birds famous for their bright pink or red coloration and distinctive curved bills. These social birds are filter feeders that live in flocks and are found in shallow lakes, lagoons, and salt flats in warm climates around the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Flamingos are easily recognized by their extremely long, curved necks, long thin legs, and specialized downward-bent bills used for filter feeding. Their vibrant pink to red plumage sets them apart from all other bird families.
children.funFact: Flamingos get their pink color from carotenoid pigments in the algae and small crustaceans they eat - without these foods, they would actually be white or gray!

children.description: Flamingos are large wading birds famous for their bright pink or red plumage and distinctive curved beaks. They are highly social birds that live in flocks and feed by filtering small organisms from water. All flamingo species share the unique ability to stand on one leg for extended periods and have specialized beaks for filter-feeding.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Flamingos are instantly recognizable by their long, curved necks, webbed feet, and downward-bent beaks that they use upside-down to strain food from water. Their vibrant pink coloration comes from carotenoid pigments in their diet of algae and small crustaceans.
children.funFact: Flamingo chicks are born with gray or white feathers and straight beaks, only developing their iconic pink color and curved beak shape as they mature and begin eating carotenoid-rich foods.

children.name: Phaethontiformes
Phaethontidae
Phaethon
children.description: Tropicbirds are spectacular seabirds known for their brilliant white plumage and incredibly long, streaming tail feathers that can extend far beyond their bodies. These ocean-dwelling birds are built for life at sea, with webbed feet, strong wings for soaring over warm tropical waters, and sharp bills perfect for catching fish and squid.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tropicbirds are easily recognized by their distinctive long tail streamers that flutter like ribbons in flight, along with their pristine white bodies marked with black wing patterns and colorful bills.
